MISCELLANEOUS. View OK A Field of Battle þÿ The view of a field of battle awakens the noblest sympathies of our nature. Even the stern Napoleon has had his cold heart touched by such a scene. The first survey is overwhelming ; and the heart of even the stoutest soldier shrinks within him, and sickens at the sight. On a nearer inspection, we find the dead and the dying, friend and foe, lying side by side ; their furious contest suddenly cut short by the cold hand ol death, while the cries and moans of the wounded fill our ears with sounds of lamentation and woe, and our hearts with pity and commisseration. We lament the fate of the slain, and grieve that his career is ended ; yet it is the death of the brave soldier Who has gloriously discharged his i with due respect, no matter to which dutv to his country, and whose fame remains imperishable, that calls forth our þÿ deepest grief, admiration, and gratitude. 1 Peninsular war, nor yet at Waterloo, Dulce el decorum, est pro patria mori." Consumption of Liff. during the Reign of Nicholas. þÿ The consumption of human life during the reign of the Emperor Nicholas has been enormous. He has carried on war with the Circassians uninterruptedly for 28 years, at an annual cost of 20, 0U0 lives on the Russian side alone, making a grand total of nearly 600,000 Russians who have perished in attempting to subdue the independence of Circassia. In the two campaigns against Persia, as in the Hungarian campaign þÿ paigns of 1831 32, there are not suffi- and the two Polish camcient data to enable me to form a correct estimate of the Russian loss, which was, however, in the Persian and Polish wars, enormous. In the two campaigns against Turkey of þÿ1828 20, 300,000 fell, of whom, however, 50,000 perished by the plague. The loss of the Russians in various ways, since the entry of the Danubinn principalities, is understated at 30,000. In these calculations it should he borne in mind that no estimate is attempted to be made of the sacrifice of human life on thesideof those who fought for their liberties against the aggressions of Russia. If this calculation were attempted, it is probable that the result would prove that neither Julius Csesar, nor Alexander, nor even Tamerlane, has been a greater scourge to the human raee than the present Emperor Nicholas. þÿ The Emperors Alexander and Nicholas, by Dr. Lee.

Sumluy Liquor Traffic. The readers of the Tidcnde are doubtless before this aware that last Sunday evening three sailors were drowned in the harbour, and thus unprepared to meet their God were sent into His presence almost in a moment of time. Two of these were in a state of beastly intoxication ; the third was an innocent boy, who had been sent with the boat to take them off to the vessel. Two others narrowly escaped the same fate. The accident occurred by the upsetting of the boat in the fighting of these drunken men. It is the proper fruit of rum-selling on Sunday, which is carried on here to an extent disgraceful in itself, and highly detrimental to the morals both of town and harbour. We understand that a petition is being or about to be circulated among the merchants to be presented to the Government, for the closing of rum shops on that day. This measure must commend itself to the moral, and no less to the financial sympathies of all good citizens. Sunday is the one day in all the week when Masters of vessels are accustomed to give their men liberty. The result is, that they come on shore not to en. joy a peaceable stroll around town, but to get drunk, to disturb the peace and quiet of that day, by their drunken frolics, or quarrels, to entail expense, or expensive delay upon their vessel, and as in the case of last Sunday evening to pay for their liberty with their life. The present danger of Yellow Fever from intoxication, and exposure in that state to the heat of the sun, is a special

reason why every one should sign this petition, and an additional ground for the belief which we do not hesitate to indulge, that the Government will respect the wishes of the citizens, and forthwith order the closing of the shops on Sunday. St. Thomas, 2nd Feb., 1855.
From the London Times, January 16. We can acquaint our renders this

no small astonishment, and which will give the public a new insight into the policy of Russia, and the contingencies of the war. The Crimea, at present the scene of hostilities, is a peninsula situated at the extreme south of the Russian

® & <g> x a: ATi empire, and connected, as our maps, inform us, with the continental territory by the Isthmus of Perekop. Across this isthmus, as we have hitherto understood, þÿCurlew, all Russian troops must be marched to the relief of their comrades before Sebastopol, and great stress has naturally been laid upon the expediency of blockading or occupying this important passage. The isthmus itself is but a narrow strip of land, and is traversed by a wall of masonry from sea to sea. The only access to the peninsula is through an arched gateway in this wall, and thus, as we are informed by a note in one of the best and most recent maps of the country in question, the possession of this fortified line effectually closes the Crimea against an enemy. Now, at this moment þÿ the þÿenemy advancing from ami the þÿ Teviot. the north is no other than Russia herself; and if, therefore, the Isthmus of Perekop could be occupied, the Crimea and its fortresses would be at the mercy of the allies on the single condition of dealing satisfactorily with the Russians actually in Sebastopol or the vicinity. No further reinforcements could be brought up. The Crimea would be þÿ inþÿvested far more completely than Sebastopol itself, and the whole peninsula, rather than the principal town, would be in a state of siege. Such has been hitherto the prevailing belief, and various plans have been accordingly suggested for bringing to pass a result so desirable. Turks were to be landed at Perekop and put in possession of the

line; gun-boats were to be stationed along the shore; and, altogether, it was argued that a pass so easy both to occupy and defend might be made our own with great advantage to the allied cause. Even if we could not absolutely keep out the Russians, we should, at any rate, be accurately informed of their coming, and could certify the strength of each reinforcement, and the time of its approach, for the benefit of Lord þÿRaglan s army. Why these schemes were never carried out it is unnecessary at present to inquire. What we now wish to tell the public is, that they would, one and I all, have been perfectly useless, for that the Russian Government had some time back constructed across the shallows of the Putrid Sea another great military road to the Crimea, so effectually that it is actually the better road of the two, ai d so quietly that Western Europe never beard a word ubout the matter. If the reader will take any ordinary map of the Crimea he will see that to the east of the Isthmus of Perekop there extends a species of narrow inland lake, known as the Putrid Sea, which is separated from the Sea ofAzoff by a curious dikelike strip of land, mi ning j up from the eastern corner of the Crimea, and almost, but not quite, touching the Russian continent at a point called the Straits of Genitsch. It is possible for troops advancing into the Crimea from the interior of the empire to leave the Isthmus of Perekop in their rear, to march along the coast of the Putrid Sea, to cross the Straits of Genitsch, and

then, by toiling along the whole length of the dikelike strip ahovementioned, called the Isthmus of Arahn, to enter the Crimea a few miles north of Kaffa. This route was actually taken by a Russian General in the last century, and it still forms a commercial road between the eastern parts of the Crimea and the continent. Some nine or ten years ago, however, a road was commenced, upon morning with a fact which will create i bridges and viaducts, across the Putrid Sea itself, and was completed, we believe, a considerable time before the outbreak of the present war. At what . points the communication between the two shores has been effected we cannot precisely say ; but they approach each

other so closely in many places, and the whole sea, besides being narrow, is so full of shoals and shallows, that many facilities for the undertaking were no doubt discovered. According to the information we have acquired, foundations were probably laid at favourable points of the shoals, and bridges then carried from one point to another, till the communication was complete. The road itself, now that it is finished, is said to be the best road available for the passage of troops and stores from Russia to the Crimea. For troops moving from Odessa we imagine that the Perekop route would be preferable, but for reinforcements arriving from the south-east of the empire and the country of the Cossacks the route across the shallows would be more convenient. In this case the distance between Simpheropol and the interior would be much shortened, and it is not improbable that both routes may have been recently employed when it was desired to surprise the allies with an overwhelming superiority of force suddenly brought up. Altogether, the fact thus tardily disclosed, in the filth month of our occupation, bears signal and striking testimony both to the preparations of the Russian Government for the contingency of war in the Crimea, and to the amount of knowledge we may yet have to acquire upon this and similar subjects.

JIISCELIiAAEOIJS. Here is a þÿ bit of þÿadvice to young ladies, setting forth how they may know whether a young gallant is really "courting" them, or only paying them þÿ polite þÿattentions. The confounding the one with the other has been the source of much trouble, both before and since the era of Pickwick and Mrs. Bardell : þÿ A young man admires a pretty girl, and must manifest it. He þÿcan help t doing so, for the life of him. The young lady has a tender heart, reaching out like vine-tendrils for something to cling to. She sees the admiration ; is flattered ; begins soon to love ; expects some tender avowal ; and perhaps gets so far as to decide that she will choose þÿ a white satin under thin þÿgauze, etc., at the very moment the gallant that she half loves is popping the question to another damsel ten miles off! þÿ Now the difficulty lies in not precisely understanding the difference between þÿ polite þÿattentions and the tender manifestations of love. Admiring a beautiful girl, and wishing to make a wife of her, are not always the same thing; and therefore it is necessary that the damsel should be upon the alert to discover to which class the attentions paid her by handsome and fashionable young gentlemen belong. þÿ First, then, if a young man greets you in a loud, free, and hearty tone ; if lie knows precisely where to put his hat or bis hands ; if be stairs you straight in the eye, with his own wide open ; if he turns bis back to you to speak to another ; if he tells you who made his

coat ; if he squeezes your hand ; if he eats heartily in your presence ; if lie fails to talk very kindly to your mother; if. in short, he sneezes, when you are singing, criticises your curls, or fails to be foolish in fifty ways every hour, then þÿdon fall t in love with him for the world ! He only admires you, let him do or say what lie will. þÿ On the other hand, if he be merry with every body else, but quiet with you ; if he be anxious to see that your tea is sufficiently sweetened, and your dear person well wrapped up when you go

If lie romps with your sister, sighs like a pair of old bellows, looks solemn when you are addressed by another gentleman, and in fact is the most still, awkward, stupid, yet anxious of all your male friends, you may þÿ go þÿahead, and make the poor fellow too happy for his skin to hold him ! þÿ Young ladies! keep your hearts in a case of good leather, or some other tough substance, untill the þÿ right þÿone can go on, and love, and þÿcourt, and be is found, beyond doubt ; after which you þÿ married, and happy, without the least hit of þÿtrouble. The following singular circumstance happened twelve years ago at the Astor Hous in this city. It transpired at the , time, and was published ; but it seems to us well worthy of preservation among the annals of adroit crime: A gentleman suddenly missed Ids gold watch, which was worth to him more than it could he to any body else, from association, it having been a family relic. He marveled much at its absence, for he knew he had only been in and out of the office and reading-room of the hotel since he noted the hour by it. In the hope of recovering it, he offered a reward of fifty dollars for it in the daily newspapers of the city. The same day he received a note, saying that lie could have his watch by calling at a certain obscure house in the city. After some little hesitation, he resolved to go. The watch was too valuable to him to he given up without at least this attempt to recover it. So he went. His call at the door was promptly answered by a gentlemanly-looking person, who, in reply to his inquiries, said that he had in his possession the advertised watch, and that on payment of the offered reward he would deliver it up. The loser promised to pay the fifty dollars provided he was convinced the watch was his. It was exhibited, and the gentleman recognized it at once, paid the reward, and gladly placed the recovered treasure in its place in his vest pocket. As he was turning to go away, he remarked, þÿ I am glad, as you may suppose, to get my watch back again, but I should

really be pleased to know how you took it from me." þÿ That I will inform þÿyou, readily replied the pick-pocket. þÿ Do you remember holding an animated conversation with two other gentlemen in the reading-room of the Astor House on the morning you lost your watch þÿ? þÿ I þÿdo, replied the loser. þÿ Well, do you also remember that a gentleman who stood close by, left his newspaper, drew near, and finally engaged in the discussion þÿ? þÿ Very þÿdistinctly, replied the other; þÿ and also that lie engaged in it with much þÿwarmth. þÿ Precisely, continued the narrator; þÿ and do you not remember that he at one time, in his earnestness, tapped you two or three times on the left breast, þÿthus? (suiting the action to the word.) þÿ þÿYes, replied the gentleman. þÿ Then I took your þÿwatch, said the other; and turning, shut the door and j disappeared.

<© m <© It 'JL A T 3 The gentleman returned to the Astor, musing on this strange occurrence ; and while relating it to some of his wondering friends, was astonished to find that his watch was again missing ! When the adroit knight of the nimble fingers described how he had once filched from him his watch, he took it again ! So the gentleman finally lost his watch, after having paid the thief the reward for its recovery,

Importance of a good Handwriting. A bad handwriting ought never to be forgiven ; it is a shameful indolence ; indeed, sending a badly-written letter to a fellow-creature is as impudent an act ns I know of. Can there be anything more unpleasant than to open a letter which at once shows that it will require long deciphering? Besides, the effect of the letter is gone if we must spell it. Strange, we carefully avoid troubling other people with trifles, or to appear before them in dress which shows negligence or carelessness, and yet nothing is thought of giving the disagreeable trouble of reading a badly-written letter. In England, good breeding requires writing well and legibly ; with us (tiermans) it seems as if the contrary principle were acknowledged. Although many people may not have made a brilliant career by their fine handwriting, yet I know that more than a lew have spoiled theirs by a bad one. The most important petitions are frequently read with no favorable disposition, or ent irly thrown aside, merely because they tire written so badly Niebuhr.

From the Observer, January 14, 1855. CHARACTERISTICS OF THE RUS- SIAN TROOPS. ( F rom the Const itutionnd) . The battles of the Alma and Inkcrman, and the siege of Sebastopol, have enabled us to study the Russian army employed in the Crimea. Although this army is partly composed of troops from the Danube and the Caucasus, it is clumsy, not easily handled, and manoeuvres badly in presence of an enterprising enemy. Its generals always place it for bivouack, as in the field of battle, in great masses, and they do not know how to deploy it after an attack, nor when to make it resist in a thin line. The Russian infantry is very badly armed. Some companies only have carbines made at Liege ; the muskets, only recently transformed, badly kept, and with butt-ends in white wood, do not last long in a campaign. This infantry will never attain the level of the French infantry, which is really the first in the world for making war in woody or hilly countries where the general-in-chief leaves a great deal to the initiative of the soldiers and to the chiefs of corps and battalions. In the defensive, the preference must be given to the English infantry, who, under the fire of the enemy, rest immovable as a rampart. In a level and exposed country our infantry will have to modify its manner of combatting, and to resume its old one. This consists in employing compact or thin order ( eptiis ou mince), but it can only be employed with intel'igent and experienced troops. Its superiority in arms and intelligence will, however, always give to our infantry the advantage

over the Russian infantry, which will always lose half its value when obliged to change its place rapidly. On the Alma, entire Russian battalions took to flight, in surprise at the þÿZouaves way of fighting, they having advanced ou them in large bodies, deployed, having taken advantage of all the accidents of the ground to shelter themselves and to rally, and having made against the masses a terrible use of the peculiar arms confided to their skill. At Inkcrman, in the upper part of the battle field, and on the line of the English, the Russian infantry bravely attacked the enemy, but did not know how to deploy its masses so as to bring more muskets into play, and when the French attacked their left flank entire battalions did not know how to change their position. The first ranks bravely resisted, but the following ranks fired in presenting arms. Surprised afterwards by the sharp attack of the Chasseurs þÿd Afrique, masses of men, instead of effecting their retreat by the crests of the hills, descended slowly to the lower parts of the grounds and the ravine, where they allowed themselves to be crushed almost without defence by from 1 ,000 to 1 ,200 French. The English have so well understood the advantages which troops would have in attacking either artillery or masses'of infantry in woody or hilly countries whilst preserving the order deployed by the first line ; that at Inkcrman they did not employ the order in columns, which caused them to lose so great a number of men on the

Alma. On the Alma the Russian cavalry was worse than timid ; not a charge did it attempt. At Inkerman the nature of the ground prevented it from taking part in the affair. At Balaklava it did not dare to await the charge of two squadrons of Chasseurs þÿd Afrique. The famous Cossacks have, in fact, never attempted, even in the plain, to carry off our advanced posts, of the marauders who pass our lines ; but it is said that this cavalry is but little esteemed, even in Russia. As a set off to this, the Russians really possess a great superiority both over the French and the English, and especially over the French, in their artillery. The Emperor Nicholas, in, no doubt, the expectation of a war against all the nations of the south of Europe, occupied himself a good deal with that arm, which has

3 T <© Ifc ® a 21 A Y :£ 3 made great progress since the wars at the beginning of the century. The cannon are of a large calibre, the carriages and caissons well made and easily moved ; the artillerymen are brave and accustomed to their service ; the officers know perfectly well how to choose offensive and defensive positions ; they occupy them with boldness , hold them a long time, and know how to leave them without leaving their guns. You will nowr understand why we are still before the walls of Sebastopol, and why that place would cost us so much blood, if we were to make an assault before its un extinguished batteries. Rut we hope that the town will surrender, in consequence of the difficulty it is under of obtaining supplies of provisions, or that we shall obtain its keys by giving a grand battle to the army in the field. The stores of ammunition in Sebastopol are inexhaustible, and, as the investment is not complete, the garrison can be relieved and increased every day. \\ ithout being initiated iu the secrets of the generals-in-chief, everything causes us to believe that they are waiting the arrival of the reinforcements which are on their way, in order to resume the attacks which, so to speak, have been suspended since the day of the battle of Inkerman. We shall have in the French and English trenches at least 300 pieces, which will open their fire, and it is more than probable that in the meantime the army of observation will destroy in a battle the Russian army in the field.

nnCULIiANY. THE BEARD AND MOUSTACHE. Our Newspapers abound with communications from different individuals, making altogether a lengthened catalogue of the various benefits which accrue from the unshaven chin and lip. Acj cording to these letters to it has been prac- tically demonstrated be a cure for quinsev, a remedy for rheumatism in the face, a protector from dust and deleterious gasses, a respirator of matchless worth, and relief from asthma and for all diseases of the lungs. In short, not a case can be cited where it has not been of eminent service ; and yet so sensitively squeamish are we, and so perverted in our judgments, that the moustache is looked upon as lit only for a ruffian, and a beard is considered the peculiar properly of a goat ! Mr. Rowland in his work on the hair, remarks : þÿ " The caprice of fashion alone forces the Englishman to shave oil those appendages which give to the male countenance that true masculine character indicative of energy, bold daring, and decision. We may ask witJi Beatrice þÿ ' What manner of man is he ? Is his head worth a hat, or is his chin worth a heard ?' 1 have noticed the whiskers and beards of many of our most eminent physicians and merchants encroaching upon their former narrow boundaries, while it is well known that not a few of our divines have been long convinced of the folly of disobeying one of Nature's fixed laws; but hitherto, their unwillingness to shock the prejudice of their congregations have prevented them from giving effect to

their convictions." A working man puts the following queries : " May not shaving, by depriving the lungs of the male of their natural protection, and exposing them to the uninterrupted action of cold air, tend to

being transmitted in an increasing proportion from generation to generation, at length induce consumption or a consumptive tendency þÿ? Do not the leaders of the faculty approve of moustaches, and are they not of opinion that they play a most important part in the animal economy? Is it not probable that by unduly stimulating the growth of the hair by shaving, we draw too largely on, and so cause an unnatural action of the nerves, producing an injurious effect (no matter how slight) on the brain? Did not the patriarchs and sages of old wear beards, and were they not remarkable for longevity as well as for being exceedingly fine looking fellows? þÿ Is not shaving a bore, and does not a man whilst undergoing the operation look extremely ridiculous? and if it is right to rasp the chin, why not the eyebrows and head also? þÿ Does it not appear foolish to shave off on a cold morning that which Nature has provided to protect us against the cold? þÿ Do we not at once despise and hold too cheaply a beneficent arrangement and infringe a natural law when we cut off what Providence says so plainly shall grow, for the more a man shaves the more the hair grows, even to the hour of his death. þÿ The head may become bald, but the face never." A railway official writes to say that he knows that wearing the beard above and below the mouth is a very great protection to the throat and lungs, and since lie did so has had fewer complaints

in those vulnerable parts, and no outbreakings on the lip when be caught cold. Many " Private Soldiers" complain of being compelled to rasp their upper lips and chins with blunt razors, while the horse-soldiers are allowed to wear their whiskers and moustaches as nature designs. They cannot see any good reasons for cavalry men being so privileged. A writer a few days since recommended that ail friends to the cause of humanity should renounce the razor from the 1st January. " If that condition be faithfully observed," says another Bearded Lion, "the doings of 1851 will sink into insignificance compared with the spectacle presented to the world by the strong minded men of 1854. þÿ St. Lucia Palladium.

Among the curious things brought to light by an Albany Health Committee, in search of the causes of the cholera, was a strange history of an Irish widow's any thing ever recorded in pig, that altogether and entirely " owld Ire- beats land." fn one house, somewhere in the suburbs, was found an indefinite num! cr of poor families, remarkable for their squnlidness þÿ their wretched poverty. One floor after another was examined, until the officers reached the " illigant accommodations" in the garret. Here every room þÿ and there were several þÿ was looked into, until one door was blockaded by a buxom widow, who seemed to be determined her apartment should be sacred. The determination, however, was invalid, and the door was thrown open, when, to the astonishment of the "Committee," there was found living in this airy abode, not only the widow aforesaid, but an immense hog, weighing over two hundred pounds. One of the gentlemen, remembering the rickety state of the narrow stairs, asked, with much curiosity, " how this great unwieldy animal had been brought up to its then lodging place?" "It was not brought here at all," said Biddy, with triumph; "it was born in this very room !" No imagination was ever equal to this romantic fact ; no American ideas of lite could conceive of such household inmates; and yet this beast had been thus reared, and the human beings under the same roof, in their selfish, noisy, death-producing apartments, never discovered its presence.

The following novel expedient for catching a thief was adopted in a provincial town in England some twenty years " ago A miller residing near a place called : Beverly, whose premises had been entered for some time previously almost, every night, and a considerable quantity of grain abstracted, hit upon a very ingenious expedient for the detection of the offender : " The means of ingress was by putting a finger through a hole in the door, which uplifted a latch. On the night in question the miller set a large foxtrap, and hung it inside the door, so that the thief would be obliged to touch the spring in opening " the door. Having taken this precaution, lie left it for the night, and on going the following morning bis expectations were realized, by finding a fellow suspended from the door by his finger! The miller, after severely admonishing the thief for his crime, and taking into consideration the sufferings the poor wretch had undergone, gave him the choice of abiding by the law, or receiving a good horsewhipping. " It is needless to add, that lie preferred the latter alternative, which the miller administered, with the full power of a stalwart arm. The writer, a correspondent of a provincial paper, who witnessed the punishment states, that with every lash the culprit's body 'crouched to the earth, and almost doubled up with the ccstacy of pain!"'

Tit INI DA I). Venezuela. þÿ Our last accounts from that neighbouring State are interesting. The Government of St. Thomas has detained the two vessels belonging to the ex-General I'acz, which were loaded with muskets, swords and ammunition of war, and destined for a new attack against the Republic. All the cargo has been landed, so that all fears of an invasion are now done away with. The other tidings are, that the elections for the Presidentship for (lie next period, have been decided, and <dl the electoral colleges have voted unanimously for General Tadco Monagas , the rival of ex- General l'aez, and brother to the present president. W e congratulate our neighbours, and rejoice at both these auspicious events, which no doubt announce happier prospects to Venezuela. The measure taken by the Government of St. Thomas, and the unanimous elections, give such a weight and moral opinion to the new president that their efforts must be the checking and defeat of all the plans projected by the enemies of Monagas ; and order and tranquility will be restored to that country which only wants a few years of peace and tolerable government to increase in power, wealth and prosperity. Venezuela possesses wonderful resources, which if developed by good sense and liberal policy, will make her probably the first State of South America. Kxandner.

The þÿ AVIS. Christiansted, Friday the 1 91 h January 1855. Tins morning, between the hours of three and four, the inhabitants of this town were roused from their slumbers by the cry of Fire! Fire! þÿ Upon their rushing 1o t heir windows, the intense light and reflection soon convinced them of the sad reality of the cry. A rush immediately took place in the direction of the llamcs, and then it was discovered that the kitchen in the yard of the house No. 2 and 3 Fisher Street, in this town, stood in one sheet of flame, and that the fire was extending itself along a fence to a neighbouring house. A few intrepid persons were actually tearing down, by their hands, the fence and other parts not wholly consumed. A fire engine soon reached the spot, brought up by the inhabitants, and commenced playing upon the fire: which was happily soon put under to some extent. The military engine then came up and assisted in extinguishing the burning embers. As usual, the female portion of the labouring class took an active part in the extinguishing of the fire, by their j readiness in procuring water and tilling the engines. It was, however, sad to notice what

3 tr <0 U D 1 'JL AT! 3 wretched tire-hooks were brought to the spot. They actually broke in pieces as soon as they were hooked on. We cannot forbear here to make a few remarks on a subject, which perhaps has escaped the notice of some. We allude to our night-watchmen. It is perhaps generally known, that two such individuals patrol the streets every night, while the inhabitants are at rest, for the purpose of being able to detect any fire, before this dreaded element gets the mastery. Here we have a kitchen, in one blaze from top to bottom ; surrounded by scores of wretchedly dilapidated houses; the sky illumined to some extent; the trees, and other elevated objects, red with the reflection of the fire þÿ and where were our watchmen? The dogs, it is said, by their howls awoke the neighbours, while perhaps our watchmen were þÿ þÿ Gentlemen where they ought not to he. From the hold which the fire had taken of the building, it is evident that it must have been burning some hours before it was discovered. Had these watchmen passed the spot hut once, after the hour of midnight, they must have detected the fire by their noses, if not by their eyes. What must we then conclude: that they had not been in that neighbourhood for the night, and consequently were negligent of their duty. This is a sail reflection ; especially when we consider, that this is the first instance, since the establishment of this regulation, that we have had occasion to test the benefit of the same.

THE þÿQUEEN S PEECH. þÿ My Lords and Gentlemen : þÿ I have called you together at this unusual period of the year, in order that, by your assistance, I may take such measures as will enable me to prosecute the great war in which wc arc engaged with the utmost vigour and effect. This assistance 1 know will be readily given ; for I cannot doubt that you share my conviction of the necessity of sparing no effort to augment my forces now engaged in the Crimea. The exertions they have made and the victories they have obtained are not exceeded in the brightest pages of our history, and have filled me with admiration and gratitude. þÿ The hearty and efficient co-operation of the brave troops of my ally, the Emperor of the French, and the glory acquired in common, cannot fail to cement still more closely the union which happily þÿ It is with satisfaction I inform you subsists between the two nations. that, together with the Emperor of the French, I have concluded a treaty of alliance with the Emperor of Austria,

from which l anticipate important advantages to the common cause. þÿ 1 have also concluded a treaty with the United States of America, by which subjects of long and difficult discussion have been equitably adjusted. þÿ These treaties will be laid before you. þÿ Although the prosecution of the war will naturally engage your chief attention, I trust that other matters of great interest and importance to the general welfare will not be neglected. þÿ I rejoice to observe that the general prosperity of my subjects remains uninterrupted. The state of the revenue affords me entire satisfaction ; anil I trust that by your wisdom and prudence you will continue to promote the pro. gress of agriculture, commerce, and manufacture. of tiif, Housf. of Commons : þÿ In the estimates which will he presented to you I trust you will find that ample provision has been made for the exigencies of the public service. þÿ My Lords and Gentlemen : þÿ I rely with confidence on your patriotism and public spirit. 1 feel assured that in the momentous contest in which we are engaged you will exhibit to the world the example of a united people. Thus shall we obtain the respect of other nations, and may trust that, by (lie blessing of God, we shall bring the war to a successful þÿtermination. The passage relative to the victories of the Crimea, which her Majesty declared had filled her with gratitude and admiration was delivered with graceful emotion. Her Majesty, having delivered her Speech, rose, and, giving her hand to
Prince Albert, left the house. The assembly then dispersed. OPENING OF THE FRENCH LEGIS- LATIVE SESSION.

SPEECH OF THE EMPEROR. PARIS, December 2(5, 1K34. þÿ E M SSI EU rs les S en a tel Its þÿ M ESS I F. U R s Deputes, þÿ Since you last met, great facts have been accomplished. The appeal which I made to the country to cover the expenses of the war was so well responded to, that the result even surpassed our hopes. Our arms have been victorious in the Baltic and in the Black Sea. Two great battles have shed lustre upon our flag. A striking testimony has proved the intimacy of our relations with England. The British Parliament lias voted thanks to our generals and to our soldiers. A great empire, rejuvenated by the chivalrous sentiments of its Sovereign, lias separated itself from the Power which, for forty years, has menaced the independence of Europe. The Emperor of Austria has concluded a treaty þÿ defensive at present, soon perhaps offensive þÿ which unites his cause to that of France and England. þÿ Thus, gentlemen, the longer the war continues, the more numerous becomes the number of our allies, and the closer are drawn the bonds already formed. What firmer bonds can there, in tact, be, than those bearing the names of victories belonging to the two armies, and recalling a common glory þÿ than the same anxieties and the same hopes agitating the two countries þÿ than the same views and the same intentions animating tintwo Governments in every corner of the globe. Thus the alliance with England is not the result of a passing interest anil of a policy of circumstance; it is
the union of two powerful nations associated together for the triumph of a

cause in which, for more than a century, their greatness, the interest of civilisation, and, at the same time, the liberty of Europe, are engaged. Unite, then, with me on this solemn occasion to thank here, in the name of France, the British Parliament for its cordial and warm demonstration, and the English army and its worthy commander for their valiant co-operation. þÿ Next year, if peace should not have been re-established, I hope that I shall have to render similar thanks to Germany, the union and prosperity of which we desire. þÿ I am happy to pay a just tribute of praise to the army and to the fleet, which, by their devotion and discipline, have worthily responded to my expectations, in France as in Algiers, in the North as in the South. þÿ to the Up present moment, the Army of the East has had to suffer, and has overcome everything þÿ disease, fire, tempest, and privations. A citadel incessantly reprovisioned, defended by aformidable artillery by land and sea þÿ two hostile armies, superior in number þÿ nothing could weaken its courage or impede its impetuosity. Let us then declare together that the army and the licet have well deserved the praise þÿ War, it is true, entails cruel sacrifi- of their country.

ces, yet everything commands me to push it on with vigour; and, with that object in view, I count upon your assistance. þÿ The land army consists at present of 581,000 soldiers and 1 13,000 horses ; the navy, of 62,000 sailors on board ship. The following is the text of the Treaty of Alliance between her Majesty the Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, his Majesty the Emperor of Austria, and his Majesty the Emperor of the French, signed Vienna, at December 2, 1854, and the ratifications of which were exchanged at Vienna on the 14th of December, 1854: þÿ Her Majesty the Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, his Majesty the Emperor of Austria, and his Majesty the Emperor of the French, being animated with the desire of terminating the present war at the curliest possible moment, by the re-establishment of general peace on solid bases, affording to the whole of Europe every guarantee against the return of the complications which have so unhappily disturbed its repose ; being convinced that nothing would be more conducive to that result than the complete union of their efforts until the common object which they have in view shall be entirely attained ; and acknowledging, in consequence, the necessity of coming to an immediate understanding with regard to their respective positions, and to arrangements for the future ; have resolved to conclude a Treaty of Alliance, and have for that purpose named as their Plenipotentiaries : (Here follow the names and titles of the Plenipotentiaries, and the intimation that they have agreed to and signed the following articles :) Article I. þÿ The High Contracting Parties refer to the declarations contained in the Protocols of the Sltli of

April and 23rd of May, of the present year, and in the Notes exchanged on tin 8th of August last; and as they reserved to themselves the right of proposing, according to circumstances, such conditions as they might judge necessary for the general interests of Europe, they I engaged mutually and reciprocally not to enter into any arrangement with the Imperial Court of Russia, without having first deliberated thereupon in com-
Article II. þÿ His Majesty the Emperor of Austria having in virtue of the

treaty concluded on the 14th of June last with the Sublime Porte, caused the i Principalities of Moldavia and Wallachia to be occupied by his troops, he engages to defend the frontier of the said Principalities against any return of the Russian forces ; the Austrian troops shall for this purpose occupy the positions necessary for guaranteeing those Principalities against any attack. Her Majesty the Queen of the United Kingdom ot Great Britain and Ireland, and his Majesty the Emperor of the French, having likewise concluded witli the Sublime Porte, on the 12th of March, a treaty which authorises them to direct their forces upon every part of the Ottoman empire, the above-mentioned occupation shall not interfere with the free movement of the Anglo French or Ottoman troops upon these same territories against the military forces or the territory of Russia. There shall he formed at Vienna between the Plenipotentiaries of Austria, France, and Great Britain, a commission to which Turkey shall be invited to send a plenipotentiary, and which shall be charged with examining and regulating every question relating either to the exceptional and provisional state in which the said Princiif>lities are now placed, or to the free passage of the different armies across their territory Article HI. þÿ In case hostilities should break out between Austria and Russia, her Majesty the Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, his Majesty the Emperor ol Austria, and his Majesty the Emperor

of the French, mutually promise to each other their offensive and defensive alliance in the present war, and will for that purpose employ, according to the requirements of the war, military and naval forces, the number, description, and destination whereof shall, if occasion should arise, be determined by subsequent arrangements. Article IV þÿ In the case contemplated by the preceding article, the High Contracting Parties reciprocally engage not to entertain any overture or propo sition on the part of the Imperial Court of Russia, having for its object the cessation of hostilities, without having come to an understanding thereupon between themselves.

Article V. þÿ In case the re-establishment of general peace, upon the bases indicated in Article I. should not be assured in the course of the present year, her Majesty the Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, his Majesty the Emperor of Austria, and his Majesty the Emperor of the French, will deliberate without delay upon offer tual means for obtaining the object of their alliance.

Article VI. þÿ Great Britain, Austria, and France, will jointly communicate the present treaty to the Court of Prus sia, and will with satisfaction receive its accession thereto, in case it should promise its co-operation for the accomplishment of the common object. Article V II. þÿ The present treaty shall be ratified, and the ratifications shall be exchanged at Vienna in the space of a fortnight. In witness whereof the respective Plenipotentiaries have signed the same, and have affixed thereto the seal of their arms. From the Observer, December 31, 1854. BALAKLAVA, Dec. 13. Yesterday night the Russians again made a sortie on the French lines, which, as usual, was repulsed. The enemy again came from the Garden Battery, but evidently with but feeble hopes of making a conquest. Fortunately, as it became dusk an unusual number of troops were observed in rear of the Russian lines, and this fact, coupled with other signs observed by our out pickets, led the allies to make preparations to defeat any attempt upon the trenches. Between nine and ten in the night the enemy, from 1,500 to 2,000 strong, sallied forth, and were instantly received by heavy volleys of musketry by the French; the Russians halted for a moment, then perceiving that our allies were quite prepared, abandoned their intention, and, instead of retreating to the town, kept along to the right, as if to take our Green Mound battery in flank. But with us they fared no better; our covering parties were on the alert, and kept up a heavy skirmishing fire, which the enemy tried to return as they hurried on. The latter was an unfortunate defence for them, as it showed their true position to both English and French batteries, which instantly opened a smart cross tire full into their already disordered ranks. The enemy made an ineffectual attempt to return lie fire of the batteries with musketry, but after a short resistance broke and dispersed in all directions. No further attempt was made that night; and, indeed, I imagine the Russians will soon give up sorties alto-

gether. As yet they have met with nothing to encourage them in such a mode of attack ; not one of their sallies have been attended with even temporary success. The Russian army under Liprandi, which for so many weeks has been our near neighbour at Balaklava, still haunts the favoured spot. They have only withdrawn about two miles and a half from their old cantonments in the plain. About 25,000 appear to have there fallen hack to the south, while a corps d'armee , 15,000 or 20,000 strong, has posted itself near lnkerman þÿ very close to the spot from which such a desperate attack was made on our right on the 5th of November. þÿLiprandi s object in thus dividing his force is not known, though as far as I can conjecture, it seems as if an attack vere meditated on our advanced battery it lnkerman. Surely, they cannot hope o surprise us a third time. No matter vhat may be said to the contrary, 1 am |uite convinced þÿLiprandi s force has been lately strengthened. When lie first ittacked our entrenchments, on the 25th >f October, he had 38,000 men, and now, when he must have lost considerably from sickness and other causes, he has, at least, 45,000 with him þÿ that is, counting the force at lnkerman and on the Tchernaya. Finer weather seems now to have set in. Cavalry and artillery in two or three days more will be able to manoeuvre on any ground, and then you may expect news of another battle. Depend upon it, 45,000 men, under an able general, will not stay quiet in their cantonments,

watching us destroying Sebastopol, without some desperate efforts to relieve the place and raise the siege. The 34th Regiment, 1,000 strong, has arrived from Corfu ; 3,500 French have also landed at Kcrson. All kinds of provisions are at famine prices. 14s. for a goose, 7s. Oil. for fowls, 5s. a pound lor ham, and so on.

Communication To the Editor of the St. Croix Avis ! Dear Sir, With regard to your editorial in vour last number, regarding the fire of Friday, I beg leave to offer a few remarks. On account of pecuniary reasons, only two watchmen patrol the town every night. Their beat l understand have been divided into 3 parts, in each of which they patrol one hour, and remain the intermediate time in the guardhouse of the Courthouse. The night in question, 1 understand, they started as usual at 11 þÿo clock and patrolled for an hour their first beat in Watergut and surrounding quarter. Their next beat commenced at 1 þÿo clock, and Queen Street was their boundary. Their last beat, which was to commence at 3 þÿo clock was to have been the remaining part of the town towards the hills, in which quarter the burning premises are situated. Thus it will be seen that the watchmen could not have passed the spot, until after 3 þÿo clock, if it even can lie presumed, that they in the hour allotted them can pass through every street in their beat. The fault lies thus more in the system, than in the watchmen. The system is faulty from pecuniary causes. However in my humble opinion it is better to have a defective night patrol, than none at all, and although I coincide with yon in regretting its want of usefulness on this occasion, I beg leave to remark, that it has proved useful on other occasions, such as the detection of thefts and the securing of the thieves. Hoping that these remarks may con-
tribute to the amendment of the system in question, I remain, Yours very truly # # #

We ave just had the most distressing h news down from the Crimea, þÿ the total loss of a great many of our transports in a heavy gale of wind. I send you a list of the vessels lost : þÿ The Prince, screw-steamer, went down, and only five were saved out of 150. The Melbourne, dismasted. Her þÿMajesty s steamer Retribution lost all her guns. Her þÿMajesty steamer s Sampson, dismasted. The Resolute gone down, and all hands lost; cargo, gunpowder. The Rip Van Winkle, lost. The AVild Wave, lost ; one boy saved. The Kenilworth, all lost. 'fhe Progress, lost ; a few saved. The Wanderer, all lost. A French ship, all lost. The Mary Ann foundered at her anchors ; all hands lost. The Pride of the Ocean, the Medora, the Sir Robert Sale, tile Lady Valiant, and the Caduccus, þÿ all dismasted. The unfortunate ships were lost just outside Balaklava. It is a most fearful coast, and a ship once on shore would not have the slightest chance, there be-

ing not a foot of beach anywhere þÿ nothing but perpendicular rocks. We luckily had gone out of the Golden Horn, above what they call the Brid ges, where only the ships that want dle of the night, and had repairing go. We dragged to in let the mid- go another anchor, and then could only hold our own. We got steam up immediately, but the breeze moderated. The Himalaya dragged also, and very nearly got on shore in the Turkish arsenal. This was last Tuesday. The Sunday before we had very heavy weather in the Horn þÿ torrents of ra n, and so cold. There was the most fearful smashing going on among the shipping. The news came down by the Valorous. Constantinople, November 20. I have to send you the news of a great calamity. On the night of ihe 13th a violent storm burst over Constantinople, and caused much damage to the loftier buildings; the mosque of the Sultan Ahmed alone losing three minarets. We were accordingly prepared for some lamentable occurrence in the Black Sea, but the intelligence received by the Valorous transcends all that had been feared. ( f the whole extent of the calamity we are still ignorant, but enough is known to give it a place among the greatest that has taken place at sea for

many years. The tempest commenced at Balaklava about seven in the morning, and in two hours eleven transports had been wrecked, and six dismasted and rendered unfit for service. The most terrible disaster is the total loss of the new magnificent steam-ship Prince, which arrived here a few days, since with the 4(ltli regiment and a cargo valued at £500,000, and indispensably necessary for the prosecution of' the siege and the comfort of the army. The loss of the Prince seems to have been partly owing to the negligence of her officers. When she arrived at Balaklava she let go one of her anchors in 30 fathoms water. It appears that the cable had never been ciinched, and the whole of it ran out ; anchor and cable were lost together. She then let go the other, ihe cable of which was so inefficiently fastened that she lost this also. She then steamed out to sea until she could get up another cable from the hold, and at last let go a smaller anchor, with which she rode until the tempest broke upon her on Tuesday morning. An eye-witness saw her carried from her moorings on the rocks with such force that in ten minutes there was hardly a piece a yard long remaining. She might also be said to go to powder. Of a crew of 150 only six were saved. This splendid vessel of 2,700 tons was purchased by government some time since, and sent out full of most valuable stores and munitions of war. Everything is lost. With the exception of the troops, everything remained in her at the time she was dash-

ed on the rocks. The whole of the winter clothing for the men has gone down þÿ 40,000 suits of clothes, with under garments, socks, gloves, and a multitude of other articles of the kind, vast quantities of shot the in consequence, and shell, and not least medical stores sent out in consequence of the deficiencies which formerly existed. The latter were, with not uncommon negligence, stowed away under the shot and shell, j and could not be landed at Scutari. They are now lost, at a time when the

demand for them is likely to be more urgent than ever, and when the Commissariat is fully occupied in ministering to the wants of those who still remain unhurt. The other British vessels lost at Balaklava are as follows: þÿ . The Resolute, all hands lost. The Rip van Winkle, all lost. The Wild Wave, one or two saved. The Kenilworth, all lost. The Progress, some saved. The Wanderer, all lost. The Marques, all lost. The Mary Ann, all lost. The Pultowa, all saved. The Caduceus, dismasted and abandoned. 'Phe following are dismasted and unfit for service : þÿ The Pride of the Ocean. The Medina. The Melbourne, screw-steamer, Hag of Capt. Christie. The Sir R. Sale. The Minchee, and The Lady Valiant. The loss of men at Balaklava is about 340. At the moment I write the mail has just arrived, and we are still ignorant of the losses at Eupatoria, tin- Katcha, and Cherson. The Henri Quatre, 84, and the Pluto, steam-frigate, are said to have gone to pieces somewhere on the west coast of the Crimea, and a Turkish manof-war to be lost. The Turkish Hagship is certainly dismasted. The Retribution, Captain Drummond, was obliged to throw over her upper deck guns. The Duke of Cambridge was on board, and still remains there. The Vulcan rode out the storm with three anchors. The Sampson, steamfrigate, lost her masts. The Prince had her masts cut away and her steam up, but the rigging of her mi/.enmast fouled

the screw, and it could not work. The vessel then ran on shore with a terrible shock. The Resolute was laden with powder and shells for the siege. By the loss of this vessel and the Prince the British army is deprived of the means of continuing the siege for the present, even if such an idea were entertained. A later account says, the disasters of the 14th are greater even than we anticipated. THE GERMAN DIET. The following is the resolution that has been adopted by the German Diet in regard to the last additional article to the April treaty : þÿ 1. That the Germanic Diet, as a European power, acknowledges the wellknown four preliminary points, according to their apparent contents, as an appropriate foundation for paving the way to a legal and secure state of peace in Europe, and especially the first and second points, as appropriate, and to be maintained from the point of view of' German interests. 2. That in accordance therewith the stipulations for peace should be pursued with energy on this principle. 3. That on the other side, however, an attack on Austria, be it on the Imperial territory, or against its troops in the Principalities, engages the whole of Germany to support Austria with all its available means. 4. In consequence whereof, and in consideration of the increasing menacing aspect of European affairs, the military committee shall be charged to take the necessary steps for appropriate federal military readiness. 5. And also that the two combined committees for oriental and military affairs shall be empowered to concert such propositions as may be deemed requisite for carrying out all military measures commensurate with necessities. þÿ Observer, December 17.

IKON BATTERIES FOR TIIE BALTIO. Some weeks since it was announced that our Government contemplated, through the suggestions of the French Government, ordering a number of floating batteries, to be constructed of wood, and cased with iron plates, as an auxiliary force to the allied fleets in the Baltic.' The batteries are to be forty in number, and are to be ready in March next. They will be flat-bottomed, with round stem and stern, and nearly 2,000 tons burden, 180 feet long, ->G feet wide, 20 feet deep, and propelled by horizontal engines of 200-horse power. The strongest materials are to be employed in the building of these formidable engines of war, and in their construction the resources of Liverpool have not been overlooked. The Mersy Steel and Iron Company, at the south end of the town, have received a large order for the manufacture of the casing plates, and the workmen are now engaged upon them night and day. A considerable portion of the plates has already been completed, and sent per rail to London. Each of

the plates is 12 feet long, 3 feet wide, and 4i inches thick ; and each battery will require 700 tons of these plates. From experiments which have been made, anil of which these batteries are the result, it has been found that the strength of iron increases enormously in proportion to its integral thickness as compared with the same amount of metal in laminae, or single plates, however closely or firmly they may be united. As, for instance, 8 inch boiler plates, strongly bolted together, being exposed to the fire of ordinary artillery, each shot perforated the mass with certainty and ease ; but when a 4-inch wrought iron plate was subjected to the same test, it was found completely shot proof, and even the heaviest shot directed against it at a distance of 300 yards, was shattered and broken like a snowball against a stone wall. These new flatbottomed gun-boats are to be armed with twelve of the largest Lancaster guns. Each boat will have two decks, the upper being bomb-proof, eight inches thick, and the lower will be the fiirhting deck. A number of these boats are already in a forward state, and the whole, no doubt, will be ready by the time they will be required by the Government. There is every reason to believe, from the experiments which have been made, that these enormous floating batteries will be more than a match for the formidable Russian forts in the Baltic; and early in the spring of next year, it lushould not give way in the interval, the Czar will find himself outwitted, after
all his years of labour and expense upon his supposed impregnable strongholds. þÿ Ibid.

From the Observer, December 10, 1854. WRECK OF T1IE FRENCH 100-GUN SHIP HENRI IV. The following letter lias been received from the Abbe Bertrand, Chaplain of the Henri IV., on the occasion of the wreck of that vessel: þÿ Off the coast of Eupatoria, Nov. 18. þÿ Our magnificent ship was wrecked on the 14th at six þÿo clock in the evening. The tempest commenced at seven in the morning, and, in spite of all our care, our activity, and our energy, we had to yield to its violence. Since our arrival in the bay of Eupatoria we had two anchors thrown out, because the approach of winter was felt, and it was necessary to guard against the bad weather. When the hurricane came on the captain had out a third anchor and a fourth. We thought we should be able to resist. Alas, no! The Henri IV., was destined to share the fate of several other vessels that were hourly broken to pieces on the coast. The sea was furious, and bellowed so as to prevent us from bearing each other, and the ship groaned beneath the blows she received from it. The whole of the furniture was flung from one part to the other with the rapidity of a railroad. I had remained in the þÿcaptain cabin s after breakfast, and while he was on the quarter-deck in order to direct the movements of the vessel, every article in the room was Hung from one side to another, and for my own part I was near losing my senses. We resisted for a good while ; though two of our chains had broken, we held on with two, and the wind began tocalm down. But what a sad thing it was to

see the beach, on which a dozen merchant vessels had been just dashed to pieces. Alas! such also was the fate reserved for us. About half-past five þÿo clock, the captain and I were about to sit down to dinner, when all of a sudden we felt a shock, and a man rushed in and cried out, þÿ Captain, the two last chains have just been broken. þÿ The two chains broken þÿ! the captain said, þÿ impossible! He went up on deck again, which he had only left five minutes before. It was but too true þÿ the ship was on her beam ends. There was no further hope ; the sea and the wind were too violent for ns to hope to get out to sea. We had only to resign ourselves , to our fate. All that was left for us was to be thrown on that part of the coast where the bottom was sandy. You cannot have an idea of the anguish we all felt, expecting every moment the first shock when the ship touched the ground. We did feel the first shock, the second, the third, aid yet the good ship held out. We were aground, but we knew not at what distance from the shore, as we were in darkness. The weather continued awful. At last the day dawned, and we found ourselves at 200 metres from the shore, and our ship had not a single drop of water in her hold. At some yards from us a Turkish vessel had been wrecked at eleven þÿo clock at night, three hours after us. She drove on a bank, which threw heron her side, and the whole of the crew we saw clinging to the masts and shrouds, not being able to remain on the deck, which was

completely under water. At last, after a night passed in indescribable anguish, fearing each moment that the ship was opening asunder, the day dawned, and we found ourselves so near land that, in the event of any great accident occurring, it would not be difficult to save ourselves. Fortunately our ship is new, five years having scarcely elapsed since she was launched. We shall all be saved, as well as the stores. We are, however, on the þÿenemy c s oast, and the

8 3T AT Cossacks, who crowded down to us in the morning, have been received with musketry. 1 do not think they will return in haste. Oil! that Sebastopol were once taken ! Perhaps we are to remain here until the ship is got oft', and she is so noble and so beautiful a vessel that it would be a pity to abandon her. For the present, however, we have nothing to þÿfear.

THE BRITISH SOLDIER. In times past it used to be plainly asserted that the worst man made the best soldier, and, though that reproach upon the profession of arms has long been retracted, there are probably still persons who think that dispositions of a reckless, irregular, lawless, or somewhat immoral turn, are those among which the recruiting sergeant finds his best account. Such persuasions, however, should have been most effectually confuted by the letters from the ranks. Every one must have been impressed with the evidence thus supplied of the character of the British soldier. It is really quite impossible that any men in any profession of life could have written in a tiettcr spirit, willia more unaffected sincerity, or with a more entire absence of any unbecoming sentiment. Conspicuous above all other features is the tone of religious feeling by which the majority of these communications arc distinguished. Almost every soldier who writes to his parents or his friends alludes to the uncertainty of life before the guns of the enemy, expresses his thankfulness for the protection vouchsafed to him, and records his unshaken trust in that Providence by which he has been hitherto preserved. And with all this there is no uncharitableness þÿ no expression of animosity against the foe þÿ no spirit of rancour or fanaticism. Our adversaries, it is said, are persuaded by their officers and their priests that they are fighting for the cause of religion against fiends in human shape, and
are taught, while they carry crosses and images about their persons, to murder
G U4 0 I A '/ their opponents as they lie wounded and helpless on the field. Contrast this spirit with that of the British soldier, sen-

with a consciousness that his life is in the hands of God, but abstaining from any sentiment of malice or vindictiveness, and nerved to the discharge of his perilous duties by the aid of principle alone.

Schools upon Hit Sabbath. No institution contributes more to the peace, prosperity, morals and respectability of a community than its Sunday schools. The law can only punish, | while Sabbath schools prevent crime. Colleges, seminaries and public schools it is true enlighten the mind and develop mental genius, but the especial object of the Sabbath school instructions are the heart, the life, the destiny, the soul. The natural demand of the soul for a religion of some sort þÿ for a Divinity to do homage to, is far greater than the aspirations after fame or wealth. A kind heart is more to be desired than a wise head, where the two qualities cannot be combined. The conquest of genius are as the flashing of livid lightning, that cracks the gloomy thunder cloud and leaves the world to wonder at its power. But the heart that feels the thrill of kindness, that is good, and true, and pure, beams like the obstructed rays of mellow moonlight, upon the world, imparting pleasure, elevating the desires, subduing the passions, and leading men to imitate its virtues. Not even the family circle is so well calculated to improve the heart of a child as the instruction of the Sabbath school, for here greater truths than ever parent uttered are taught, and the child learns, what many men never learned, þÿ who is my þÿneighbor? To a faithful teacher there is no more delightful employment than to teach children þÿ susceptible as they always are þÿ the simple truths of the Bible, and when we contemplate the silent
influence which these Sabbath school instructions have in forming the future character of man or woman, the position becomes one of great importance and responsibility.

Dear Sir, When we recall to mind the encomium bestowed on Mr. Fesink in a former number of tiie Avis we cannot but agree with the publisher that it was in reality, deservedly bestowed. Our community being small, small things are easily digested. We have been visited by jugglers and a company of Minstrels who seemed to have given (with but one exception) general satisfaction. Mr. þÿFesink s performance, however, in our estimation surpasses them all. His astonishing feats on the tight wire baffles conception, and an hour spent seeing him and his company is more gratifying that hours spent in witnessing the awkward tricks of a would-he-Magician or þÿ Wizzard of the þÿNorth. Hut we have to regret that Mr. Fesink does not receive more patronage. None who has once seen the performance can say otherwise than that it is worth his while to see it. lie uses every exertion to please j the Otwaschnoi, 6, 400 horse power; the audience, and it is most surprising that he does not always have a full house. We must hope, however, that after this the inhabitants of this town will, as an encouragement, patronize, to the greatest possible extent, this small but really deserving company. Go and see for yourselves !

THE MILITARY RESOURCES OF ENGLAND. The military resources of a country are simply a question of pressure. The British empire is a perfect mine of soldiers. The Irish are only too fond of fighting in all its varieties. In Scotland there are families and districts that think themselves far too much gentlemen for any trade but the army, and who would rather run a man through the body, in any cause, or on any pretence whatever, than fit him on a pair of trowsers or dig coals for him at the bottom of a pit. In she in- j England, in that great rich stratum of tends to follow a similar course in the j society called the middle classes, and It may ; commonly supposed to be the chief staple of this country and the nursery of its enterprise, one of the commonest that, with all the gigantic resources she j incidents of private life is the determination of young Master John or Master Tom to go into the army or the navy. The determination is resisted and finally overcome by the parents on very suffiextent, both in the Baltic and the Black j cient grounds viz., that if the lad enlists þÿ into the ranks lie has hitherto had no < chance of a commission ; and a commission involves þÿ first, interest, then waiting, then a round some of money, then a large annual allowance, then the certainty of expensive habits utterly beyond the þÿlad s condition in life. The whole constitution of the army is opposed to this ambition. The usage of this aristocracy, the rules of the Horse Guards,
the system of promotion þÿ everything within the power of the Government, are dead against the generous instincts described. It is notorious that bishops

with canonries, good livings, and, by implication, pretty wives and large fortunes at their disposal, cannot for the life of them keep their sons out of the army and the navy. In vain do they offer them snug rectories with £1,200 a year and nothing to do ; the young scion of episcopacy breaks loose from chaplains, appariiors, nurses, and mamma, and is now roughing it on the Black Sea or the heights of Sebastopol. If bihops cannot keep their sons at home, I but must share the miseries of the hen charged with a brood of ducklings, a fortiori the poor parson þÿ children and £200 a-year a fortiori the with his ten tradesman and shopkeeper. Go into Waterloo House þÿ and there are fifty such houses in London þÿ and question the two hundred young men in Mack coats and white neckerchiefs, ready to suit you with a red riband or a railway wrapper, as to the secret aspirations of their boyhood, and you will find that at least 50 of them, had they been allowed their own way, would be now in her þÿMajesty suniform. But everything is done to discourage the universal passion, and confine the middle classes to their shopkeeping. þÿ Once in the ranks, always in the þÿranks, has hitherto been the maxim of our army. The man who accepts the shilling from the recruiting sergeant, and fulfils an engagement made over his ale in a pothouse, bids adieu to all hope of rising in this world. A brickþÿlayer s hodman may live to keep bis carriage ; a shopboy may become a millionaire, and a gardener an M. þÿI but ., a

common soldier must give up all ambition, and seek what pleasure he can in the most transient indulgences. It has been said that over the gates of monasteries there is w ritten what Dante places over the entrance of Hell þÿ that there is no hope there. There is no entrance in this country of which the like can be said, unless it he admission into the ranksofber þÿMajesty service. s Ami yet, without any serious attempt to mend this state of things þÿ without offering a young fellow with a taste for soldiering or sailoring any inducement beyond pay and a medal, Parliament is to give up all endeavour to extract more men from the great middle classes of this country. This, certainly, is a strange requital to that country which has forced upon the Government a war which it now admits to have been in absolute necessity. Thanks to the unanimous resolution of the people, Government is now in a position of great honour, and with a very fair prestige of success. To have repelled a Russian invasion, and helped to drive every Russian army out of Turkey ; to have carried the war into the þÿenemy c s ountry, and there, on his own soil, inflicted two signal defeats on large armies composed of his best troops, and choosing their own positions and times of attack þÿ to have established an impregnable position commanding bis great stronghold þÿ these are achievements of which any Government might be proud þÿ Ibid.

INCIDENTS OF THE WAR. The seamen of the port of Marseilles admit that they have never seen such magnificent steamers as the Ripon, Candia, and Thames. If anything could have excited the enthusiasm of the Marseillais, it would have been the style in which the Thames sailed out of the harbour, the sun shining brightly, the band of the Gist Regiment of Infantry playing, þÿ Godsave the þÿQueen, and the officers standing uncovered, but the few persons on the pier looked on in stupid amazement. Not a cheer, in fact, was raised for the gallant fellows. Fancy the Guards filthy with dirt and vermin ; the latter infest all the army more or less. Their beautiful coatees are their daily and only dress, and the 11 ussars call their splendid jackets gilded night dresses. Lord Cardigan still figures in the uniform of the lltli. The Russian banker, Baron von Strieglitz, who had been for some time at Vienna, endeavouring to induce capitalists to subscribe to the Russian loan, has taken his departure after having failed in all his efforts. So grovelling is the idolatry of the know-nothing party in America towards Russia þÿ so blind is it to the future, so lost to the lessons of the past so in- þÿ tense its hatred to France and England þÿ so little confidence does it really feel in the strength of its adored Colossus þÿ that it would rather see the whole universe plunged into chaos, through the extension of war to the United States, than that a single link should he broken in the chain of servitude which they would fain see cast over all European

people by Muscovite hands. The army of Kars, consisting of 8,000 men, is said to be in a wretched state. Colonel Williams on inspecting it, discovered that of 2,500 cavalry there are not 500 fit for active service. The artillery horses are somewhat better, but their harness is completely worn out. The sanitary condition of the army at Churuk-su is greatly improved, but it is completely destitute of cavalry. Zarif | Mustapha Pasha, commander-in-chief of the army of Kars, and Kurschid Pasha, his chief of the staff, were daily expected at Erzeroum. The Russians still occupied the Pashalik of Bajazid with a corps of 8,000 men, composed of infantry, cavalry, and artillery. General Forey, in his report to Gen. Canrobert, writes þÿ þÿ You will remark, General, by the number of officers put hors (le combat, that they were the special object of the fire of the enemy. The French officers, proud of their position, do not disguise their rank, like the enemy, under the capote of the solþÿdier. Is there any reason why the þÿsoldier s capote should not disguise the rank of French and English officers, when by signalizing if they are exposed to being shot in the proportion to their soldiers of two or three to one. Would the Duke of Cambridge have been dogged if his dress or mounting had not been unnecessarily conspicuous ? An officer, writing from the camp before Sebastopol, says: þÿ þÿ offered I £1 for a frying-pan, and thought it a low price. Fancy a Fusilier sending his ser-

vant yesterday (Nov. 9) to bid up to £10 for one þÿ! The Russians call our revolvers infernal machines, which have been given to their enemy by the devil, and imagine that they will go þÿoff whenever required by invoking his aid ; hence the great terror always evinced whenever these weapons arc brought forth.

This establishment, built on a rocky promontory to the south of Cape Chersonese, is, most delightfully situate. Unfortunately, being exposed to the first fury of the tempest, it received its full violence. The church was shaken to its foundations and much damaged. Some of the iron gates were flung down, with pieces of the wall, and the sheet-iron roofing was carried away like pieces of paper to the distance of between one and two English miles. The Czar has ordered two more battalions to be added to the regiments of j the Finland army, thus again violating the solemn promise made by Alexander to the Fins, lie has also ordered the formation of six battalions (some accounts read sixty) of rifles. The peculiarly military administration called the þÿ state of þÿwar, instituted at St. Petersburg in the spring, when our naval squadron entered the Baltic, has just been suspended.

DOMINICA. We mentioned some months ago that some printing slips had been received hereand deposited at our Reading Rooms shewing the feasibility of the new source of industry which the plantain and banana fibre held out, and that a few pounds ot the article had been shipped to England in consequence. We are pleased to report that the chief difficulty we have all along understood to he in the way, viz: the want of a Machine for drying anil threading the stems is about to he successfully overcome and that in the West Indies themselves. We have been politely favored by Frederick Garraway, Esq., of the firm of Messrs. Garraway, Sons & Co., with several specimens of fibres oft he plantain and banana trees, prepared by Messrs. Burns and Burke, of the island of iMontserrat, by means of an apparatus invented by these gentlemen. The specimens before us are certainly beautifully white and clean and the fibres are unbroken through their entire lengths. Mr. Garraway informed us that the process of bleaching the fibres was extremely simple þÿ that no chemical agents were used, and that they would he fit for packing immediately almost as they came from the apparatus; this latter is extremely simple, and with water power, we are informed, can he worked most economically. In an island like this in which the plantain and banana abound, as well as the American aloe and the penguin or ' la pile," and in which there is such an abundance of water, nothing remains to lie called into exercise but energy and

industry to realize from these sources, profitable articles of export, additional to our present ill requiting staples. The universal cry is that the cultivation of our staple articles of export þÿ Sugar, Rum, and molasses þÿ is non-remunerative, and that in addition to these other articles of export ought to lie sought after less costly in their cultivation and manufacture for the home market. We are informed that a ton of these prepared fibres will realize in that market according to their degree of purity and fineness from £40 to £60. Here then are new sources of wealth which require energy and no doubt some small amount ofcapital to develnpe them. The aloe, t he pile, and the coarser fibres of the plantain will produce fibres which can he converted into rope equal to any hitherto manufactured from Russian hemp þÿ the finer fibres of the same plantain ran lie converted into textures for clothing of the finest as well as most durable description, and experiments are being now made having for object the ascertaining whether the inner part or pulp of the plantain tree cannot lie converted into paper. Messrs. Burns and Burke seek to obtain from the legislatures of these Colonies the patent righi for the sale ot' their M acliities. This we think they are entitled to, for a limited period, lie who causes two blades ot grass to grenv where one grew before is considered to he a benefactor to his race, and as such entitled to some more substantial remuneration than simple gratitude; and they

therefore who by patient industry arrive at a discovery fraught with so much benefit to these isles of the West are entitled not only to the gratitude of their inhabitants, hut as in all similar instances, to the right to dispose of such discovery to their exclusive benefit, at least for some time. Our planting friends who may he desirous of having a view of some specimen of these fibres as prepared liy the apparatus of Messrs. Burns and Burke may gratify their wish by applying at this þÿoffice. Dominican. Nov. 15.
