From the St. Thomas Times, February 21. Tlic Conspiracy at the Havana.

By the arrival on Saturday night last of the It. M. Steam-ship Conway, Captain Vai.ler, from the Gulf of llavaua, we obtain from the latter place information of the fortunate and timely discovery of a deep-planned conspiracy directed against the Authorities and Officials of that City, and which, it would seem, had been well-conceived, and to all appearance about to be matured. At the departure of the steamer no published account had appeared, but a graphic description was anxiously looked for by the citizens from the Government organs. A Proclamation, however, had been issued by the Captain General, wherein it is announced that the designs of the conspirators had been frustrated, and that law and order prevailed over the entire country. As our information is based purely upon verbal I testimony although given þÿ with an assurance of its accuracy, and reliable in its character we þÿ must, nevertheless, be cautious in regard to particulars, and what we may relate must be received with a degre3 of hesitation. The principal and essential organization of the conspiracyappeared to rest in the charge of two persons, who, until the moment of discovery, enjoyed tho unlimited confidence of the Executive, His Excellency the Captain-General Concha, and who, from their lofty and respectable positions in the government and society, could easily, when faith was once in them reposed, command the same. These t«o persons, daily in conversation with His Excellency, comprised one Ramon Pinto,

(a Catalan), President of the College, the other Jose Echevaria (a Biscanian), President of the Railway Company, men who from the very natdre of their avocations þÿ one in developing the human mind, the other in developing the resources of the territory þÿ were most naturally of all others likely to win the admiration and es- ! teem of the man selected to personify

in the land. These two miserable recreants have already with their lives at the Garrott expiated their treachery and guilt. The execution of the plot seems to have been laid for the night of the 10th instant, when a very attractive Piece was to have been performed at the Theatre, to which tho patronage of Ilis Excellency, Suite, and Principal Officers of Government, had been secured. A railway train was to have conveyed to the City at a certain hour the assasins, who were to be conveniently placed iu the vicinity of the Governor's box. At the proper moment the Gas was to have been shut off so as to extinguish the lights, and, as the sequel, the bloody Drama was to be enacted by sacrificing the lives of His Excellency and his principal advisers ; this accomplished, and dismay and confusion thrown into the entire City, express trains were to have circulated the intelligence with all speed over the Island ; the command of the principal Military Posts and Forts it was believed could be obtained; and in a few days, vessels laden with ammunition, and carrying large bodies of men were expected to arrive at different places on the Island, which would again by the railroads have been disposed of in such manner as to have baffled the ablest efforts of the loyalists, however large in number. On the 7th it would seem the scheme became known to the Governor, and after adopting every precaution, by acquainting the Military Commandants, and dispatching the men-of-war to cruize around the Island, His Excellency satisfied

by proof of the facts that had been brought before him, and the principal actors secured, the extreme penalty of the law was brought to bear upon them, and numerous arrests were made of those to whom suspicion seemed to attach þÿ c- California Gold.

It is, however, not very important fo- the towns people to know when the repairs are to commence þÿ all they reru i re are good roads, properly shaded by trees. The roads are, we hoar, very well mended ; and with few exceptions here and there a little carelessness can be detected, which may be considered trifling. As to the trees þÿ we mean those on each side of the roads þÿ they aro not numerous ; and the want of those Thibet trees, which gave such a b nutiful shade along tin lower part ot the Centre Line, that have lately been cut down, is very much felt. l.ut lhe evil is not confined to this alone In those parts of the country where trees abound, the shade cannot be properly appreciated, as the branches hang so low as to cause destruction to carriages. These evils can he easily remedied. The respective W ay- Wardens ought, therefore, to pay a little more attention to the 2d of the second Fart of the lload Ordinance, and they will there clearly see what is much w.diting in their duty. In continuation of the Government's Publication of the 12tb of May 1852, whereby was made known that, the Instruction for the Measurement of Vessels, promulgated on the 7th February 1843 and approved of by Royal assent, has been extended to the Danish West India Possessions by Resolution of the Minister of Finance, dated the 18th of March 1852 þÿ it is hereby made known that the Rules laid down in the abovementioned Instruction, will be applicable from the 1st of April 1855. In conformity herewith all ship-owners are bound, at the request of the respective Customhouses, to submit their vessels to be re-measured if they are present at their homeplnce or as soon as they return to the same. No Fee is to be paid for such re-measurement. except in case the vessel, from other reasons, ought to be measured. To which all concerned have to conform. THE CONDITION OF THE ARMY. The accounts as to the stale of our army in the East are still very depressing, and, as the leading journal says, the first pledge that the new Government must give of its intentions to carry on the war with vigour and success is by showing, not only thai merit will be rewarded, hut that negligence and incompetence will be severely punished. The telegraphic accounts and the official despatches are a little more favourable than the description given by newspaper correspon-

dent; but it must be remembered that, however conflicting the statement may be, those of writers for the public journals have been fully confirmed. The ' Times' says,--. Day by day the thin veil winch official mystification had striven to spread over the appalling realities of our position is falling away, and a scene is disclosed the unutterable woe and misery of which the most excited imagination cannot represent, the most graphic pen cannot depict. Slowly sinking down from an abyss of misery which a short time ago would have been deemed impossible to an abyss far lower and more awful, our army seems to be reaching tfie period assigned to all human woe, as it has long ago passed the suffering hitherto believed to be the limit of human endurance. Down, down, ever downward, without an abatement or letardation, in the steady career of destruction have our soldiers sunk, and, dark as have been our prognosiics, the reality has always kept far more than pace with them. Our correspondents turn with sickening disgust from the dreary monotony of a narrative which tells of nothing but death in the shape most abhorrent to brave men---in the form of loathsome and incurable disease. Our battalions in the Crimea melt awav like the snow that surrounds their tents and fills their trenches. and this diminution of our military force is registered by a corresponding increase in our hospitals. One hospital has grown into three, three into eight, and eight into thirteen Cargo after cargo of the emaciated

relics of the survivors of our great battles has been sent to Malta, Corfu, and England. Death is clearing the hospitals at the rate of 50 or 60 a day ; but still the tide of misery overbears all the receptacles devised to contain it, and the re is no room for the immense number of patients whose arrival is immediately expected. 5000 sick are, it appears, already in the camp, and one half of those doing duty arc already unfit for work. F R A If 0 E. The ' Times' Paris correspondent writes on Thursday evening that preparations on a very extensive scale are going on in every department of the military service there. It is stated that t hey have reference to not less than three army corps, one of which is intended for the Baltic ; the other, if necessary, for the Rhine ; and the third for Austria. The polytechnic school will furnish a sufficient body of well educated officers for the artillery and engineers. The spring is the period when these corps will commence their movement. THE MINISTERIAL CRISIS. The 'Globe' says---" We have reason to believe that Viscount Canning, the postmas ter general, will be a member of Lord Palmerston's cabinet. Lord Panmure enters upon bis duties as war minister to day, im mediately after the termination of the privy council at Windsor. The noble lord has ap pointed as his private secretary Mr. George Dalhousie Ramsey, of the war office, who has been acting as private secretary to Mr. Sidney Herbert. No definite arrangements regarding Mr Layard's appointment has yet

been made, and it is not improbable that an Act of Parliament may be required, when the first lord of the treasury will probably be in his place," vv> a <<« Mliip News. þÿ The American slop Fanny Giffvey , of Kcnnebank, 7-15 tons burthen, Capt Moody, left Liverpool on the 13th January, bound to New Orleans, with a cargo of Salt. The "AVIS." Chrisliwnsted , Friday the \6th February IS 55. We have received files of Colonial Papers and from them made extracts, which will be found in our columns.

From the St. Thomas Times, February 10. .Marine Disaster. The British schooner Rose, Captain Rudolph, put into this port this morning in distress, with only the Captain and two men on board. She was bound to Demerara from Baltimore with an assorted cargo, and on the night of the 22nd ultimo þÿ 27 days out þÿ was run into by the American ship Revenue of Dennis. The night was very dark and the weather boisterous. The mainmast of the Rose was carried away, one man was drowned, and her chief mate and two hands got on board the ship þÿ but the weather was so severe that they could not be restored to their own vessel. The Revenue remained by the schooner until daylight, when they parted.

The "Columbia." The United States Frigate " Columbia," 50 guns, Commander Wilson, 34 days from Greytown, and bearing the Flag of Commodore Newton, arrived here yesterday. Salutes were exchanged between her and the Fort. The Commodore landed this morning, and was received at the King's Wharf by a Guard of Honor, and a salute from Fort Christian. He proceeded to Government House, where, we understand, he will pass a few days.

America. The American three-masted schooner lira, Captain Berry, arrived here yesterday. Her dates from New York are to the 20th January. The return of Mr. Soule from Spain, and the nomination by the Cabinet of Mr. Breckenridge as his successor, are announced by the Washington correspondent of the Courier and Inquirer. Most of the leading papers appear to denounce the course pursued by the former gentleman in his negociations with Spain, and state it as a settled fact that the present Administration will abandon its previous attitude with requestions. A special Meeting gard to the Cuban and Black had Warrior been held by the Members of the Chamber of Commerce at the Merchants' Bank, New York, for the purpose of offering Resolutions to present a Testimonial to Commodore Perry for his services in the East. The meeting was numerously attended, and the Resolutions on being submitted were unanimously adopted. A Committee was then appointed to complete the arrangements for the Testimonial, and to decide whether it should consist of a " Public Banquet" or a " Service of'Plate."

The San Fernando Gazette, in a sensible article on the recent epidemic, observes amongst other things : þÿ In pursuance of some former hints to the Government, we again draw attention to the commemoration of the dire calamity in reference to subsequent safety. We have had in our Cemeteries unmistakable evidences that a pestilence has been amongst us. We ask is it fitting or prudent for others, that the receptacles of the dead from that pestilence should be unmarked, unnoticed, and unknown ? We believe it to be becoming and prudent, and then necessary in us, for the benefit of those who may succeed us, to mark particularly the spots where the bodies cut down by Cholera are interred, lest an untimely re-opening of such spots or graves should re-awaken the dark shadowy Devastator to his work of death. We have thus, at least, so far completed our purpose in referring to the visitation of Cholera amongst us: we trust it is for the last time. Little is now heard of it, even from remote districts, and we arc sanguine in the hope that it has passed almost entirely away. It is not right however, that we should be too secure. It may come again at a time when we think not þÿ Ibid

We congratulate our fellow colonists of Demerara on their brightening pros- pects, under the " unusually fir.e weather" with which the colony had been blessed. When we say " unusually fine," our local readers will understand that the weather had become unusually dry, enabling the planters to get off some of the canes left over from last year's crop, and to put their fields in order. þÿ The health of the province continued as before. . Scarlet fever was prevailing amongst children and cold and catarrhs were pretty general. Subscriptions to the Patriotic Fund continued brisk: the amount had already reached upwards of 10,000 dollars, and it was estimated would reach 15,000 dollars by the next mail. þÿ Ibid.

From the St. Lucia Palladium, February 10. Cholera has found its way to Turks Islands, assuming however, a much milder type than what was experienced here and in the neighbouring islands. The epidemic commenced on the 18th December last, at Salt Cay, and the account extends to the 15th Jan., during which period there were 152 cases, 52 of which were fatal. The average number of deaths does not amount to 2 daily, while the greatest mortality which occurred in one day was 7 fatal cases. It is stated that the crisis of the disease had already passed and that it was abating. From St. Christopher we are happy to find the disappearance of the disease in the capital, except some isolated

cases which still prevail in the country parishes. We have been informed that H. M. Brig of War Mariner , Com. Cochrane, which left this port about a fortnight since, proceeded to Antigua to join the Calypso The destination of both ships . appears to be the island of Aves, to settle some difference with the Americans who have taken possession of that island, notwithstanding it belongs to Great Britain, on account of the guano deposited there. þÿ Ibid.

The total population of Great Britain and the islands in the British Seas is set down at 21,121,967; and if the soldiers and seamen abroad, of the army, royal navy, nndmerchant service, are excluded, 20,959,477 inhabitants remain, whose birth places are determined. It is somewhat singular that those who incur liabilities to newspaper establishments seldom apply to them the same rules regarding prompt payment which hold good in regard to other business emanations. An ingenious Montreal editor, who has it would seem, been holding some communication with the spiritual world upon this subject by means of a ricketty table in his office, gives the following as the results of his experiments: þÿ 'To put the spirits to the test, we placed before us a long list of accounts due to this office, both for subscription and advertising. We then questioned the spirits relative to our chances of being paid by each delinquent, at the same time mentioning the name, amount, and length of time we have waited for a þÿsettlement. We can assure our readers that it is more in sorrow than in anger we state the answers are very likely to prove correct. In many instances, however, we were glad to observe, for the sake of humanity, our chances are certain, while in too many there is no hope left us. When we inquired the ultimate fate of those sinners who cheat the printer, the table shook violently, the spirits became dreadfully enraged with honest round tion, the room appeared to go indigna and round with the table, was gradually filled with a strong smell of sulphur, and at

« <D It SL A T last the 'devil' entered to demand the result of our experiments. We forbear to make any further disclosures, except this, the awful fate of many will be obviated by making immediate payment.'

Anecdote of Lord Byron. þÿ The followingyt'Kx esprit (P in which Lord Byron took a part, are very little known, and, it is believed, were never before in print, Two young officers of artillery obtained leave of absence from the garrison of Malta, in the early part of the present century, to make a tour up the Mediterranean. At Athens they found the walls of a lodging-house scribbled over with names, and. among the collection, those of Sligo, Hobhouse, and Byron, under which, in an oval ring, they wrote those lines : þÿ " Fair Albion, smiling, sees her son depart, To trace the birth and nursery of art ; Noble his object! glorious his aim ! He comes to Athens, and þÿ writes his name!" Lord Byron was at Athens at the time, and a few days afterwards they found the following, side by side with the former lines, and in a similar ring. the counterpoise. "This modest bard, like many a bard unknown, Rhymes on our names, yet wisely hides his own ; And yet, whoe'er he be, to say no worse, His name would bring more credit than his verse." Byron. Under the two they then'added : þÿ " Admiring Athens, as in days of old, In these degenerate days may still behold Two rival bards contending for her cheers þÿ The name of one concealed, and one a peer's !" - Huntley's Miscellany for February.

A Thought fob Every Day þÿ We see not, in this life, the end of human actions. The influence never dies. In every widening circle it reaches beyond the grave. Every morning when we go forth, we lay the mouldering hand on our destiny, and every evening when we have done, 'we have left a deathless impress upon our character. We touch not a wire but vibrates in eternity þÿ not a voice but reports at the throne of God.

To make Water Coi.d. þÿ The following is a simple mode of rendering water almost as cold as ice: Let the jar, pitcher, or vessel used for water, he surrounded with one or more folds of cotton, to be constantly wet. The evaporation of the water on the outside will carry ofi' the heat from the inside, and reduce it towards the freezing point. In India, and other tropical regions where ice cannot be procured, this is common. The vessel should be kept covered at the top.

Habits þÿ Like flakes of snow that tall unperceived upon the earth, the seemingly unimportant events ot life succeed one and other. As the snow gathers together, so are our habits formed. No single flake that is added to the pile produces a sensible change ; no single action creates, however it may exhibit, a man's character : but as the tempest hurls the avalanche down the mountain, and overwhelms the inhabitant and his habitation, so passion, acting upon the elements of mischief which pernicious habits have brought "together by imperceptible accumulation, may overthrow the edifice of truth and virtue.

An Infallible Cure for Lowness of Spirits. þÿ Take one ounce of spirits of resolution, an equal proportion of the oil of good conscience : infuse into these a tablespoonli.il of the salts of patience, and add thereto a few sprigs oi others' woes which grow extensively in the garden of life. Gather, also, a handtul of the blossoms of hope ; sweeten these with the balm of Providence, and, if possible, procure a few drops ot genuine friendship, but be careful of counterfeits in the ingredient of self-interest, which grows spontaneously þÿ the least admixture of it with the above would spoil the composition. Reduce the whole to an electuary by a proper proportion of ot con- tent, flavor with the essence good judgment, and regulate the quantity taken according to the virulence of the disease.

A Promise. þÿ A promise should be given with caution and kept with care. A promise should be made by the heart, and remembered by the head. A promise is the offspring of the intention, and should be nurtured by recollection. A promise and its performance should, like the scales of a true balance, always present a mutual adjustment. A promise delayed is justice deferred. A promise neglected is an untruth told. A promise attended to is a debt settled.

The word, Dun, was first used during the reign of Henry VII. It owes its birth to Joe Dunn, an English bailitf, who was so indefatigable and skilful in collecting debts that it became a proverb, when a person did not pay his debts, "Why don't you Dunn him?" Hence originated the word which is in general use.

Worth Knowing. þÿ Parch half a pint of rice until it is brown þÿ then boil it as rice is usually done. Eat slowly, and it will stop the most alarming cases of diarrhoea.

A meeting of the members of the Savings' Hank was held at the Athelueum yesterday, for the purpose of exhibiting a statement of the Hank, and electing officers for the ensuing year. The annual report being unpublished, we cannot, consequently, give any information as to the number of depositors and other particulars $ but must, however, content ourselves with what appears in the weekly report, which is inserted in another part of our paper. To judge then from the total amount, $38,18 1 1 1, a s given in the weekly report, the progress of the Hank is great, and indeed it is very gratifying to notice that, within the short period it has been established, only 2 years and 9 months, so large a sum has been accumulated. The advantage sderived from such an Institution cannot be too highly appreciated, and it is certainly pleasing to see the large number of minors, with their deposit books on Saturdays, presenting themselves tit the Hank. One thing, however, is much to be regretted, there arc very few depositors among the country people, who seem not to know the benefit of a Savings' Hank. LEGISLATIVE a COUNCIL. ( Frum the Fort of Spain Gazette , January 20.) The Legislative Council met to-day for the purpose of passing the Estimates for the present year. There was a full attendance of members. The several items of the different establishments were passed without much discussion, uniil the Colonial Secretary came to the Ecclesiastical Establishment þÿ under the head of Church of Rome. The lion, gentleman moved a resolution agreeably to instructions from the Secretary of State for the Colonies, that in future the salary of the Roman Catholic Bishop should be £500 per annum instead of £1000 as heretofore. On this motion being made, the Solicitor General rose and presented a petition, most numerously signed by the Roman Catholic members of the community. The petition was read by the clerk. It prayed that the salary should lie allowed to remain at the same amount as previously, and stating sundry reasons why no reduction should be made. (The petition itself will be given in our usual Council report.) The Hon. Solicitor General addressed the Board at great length in favor of the prayer of the petition. The Attorney General and Chief Justice replied, defending the principle 011 which the proposed reduction should take place ; þÿ that as the Roman Catholic Bishop had charge of other British colonies, as also of the Danish colonies, in the West Indies, it was only fair that these colonics should contribute to the support of the Bishop, and that it was considered by the Home authorities, that £500 was the

fair proportion which should be paid from the funds of this colony. Mr. Rostant addressed the Board in an excellent speech, in favor of the prayer of the memorial. After some few observations from the Solicitor General, in reply to the Atty. General, the resolution was put, that the salary stand at £500. The resolution was carried þÿ the Chief Justice, Colonial Secretary, Attorney General, Treasury, Collector, Messrs. Hume, Wainwright and Darling þÿ 8 for ; þÿ Solicitor General, Dr. Philip, Messrs. llostant and Ginseppi þÿ 4 against. Mr. Rostant gave notice of protest On the item £500 for Inspector of Schools, Mr. Hume made some strong remarks as to the paucity of visits of the Inspector to the rural schools, instancing 10 schools which he had only paid 19 visits to in 9 months. The Chief Justice was of opinion, that the Inspector should do more than he at present did, for the salary which he was receiving. Mr. Hume urged his Excellency, that he should impress upon Mr. Anderson the necessity of more frequently visiting the Schools in the Rual Districts than he had hitherto done. Under the head of Police, a discussion took place in which the Chief Justice strongly animadverted on the want of intelligence, energy and zeal displayed by the police, an instance of which came before him, on a late occasion in the Criminal Court, and he was of opinion, that with the present Inspector they were not likely to have a better disciplined set of men. The general opinion of the

members seemed to be that the present Inspector was not fit for the situation which he held, and that it was a pity lie could not be removed to some other berth. One honorable gentleman recommended that Mr. Harrigan should be made nurse at the Colonial Hospital, but

another lion, member did not think that he would he able to perform the duties. The Colonial Secretary remarked that there were daily complaints against the Inspector. The members, generally, regretted that Mr. Thomas had been removed from the police, although the appointment he now held was more lucrative. His Excellency stated that he should not lose sight of the subject, and would take the earliest opportunity of remedying the evil complained of. It is proposed to relieve the Police of all duty connected both with the town and rural petty civil courts in serving citations, &c. This will be a great improvement, and we have no doubt will work well. The Colonial Treasurer objected to the annual grant of £250 to the Bishop of Barbados for defraying the expenses attendant on a four months' visit to the colony during each year. A resolution was moved to strike this item out, which was carried. Colonial Treasurer, Solicitor General, Messrs. Hume, Wainwright, Darling, Rostant and Giuseppi, 7. Against, Chief Justice, Colonial Secretary, Attorney General, Collector, and Dr. Philip, 5. The Attorney General gave notice of protest. On the item £l(>00 to extend and complete the new Jetty at the South Quay, Mr. Hume objected, but after some discussion the vote was carried. At the request of Mr. Darling a committee was named to report on the expediency of extending or completing the Jetty. The committee to consist of the Colonial Treasurer and Collector, and Messrs. Wainwright and Darling.

(J3® The subjoined article from the Colonist on the Demerara Exhibition, has hitherto been shut out of the Globe for want of room ; but its perusal will still aflord matter for reflection and interest to many of our readers: þÿ We have now seen the exhibition, and can speak from our own observation ot its entire success. It is calculated that since the opening of the present century, Russia has received from England upwards of tit'ty millions sterling for hemp and tibres, and surely it will not be difficult to turn that stream of commerce to the shores of her own colonies. On the fibre table were specimens of various texture, from the finest (loss of the silk cotton to the coarse barklike string of the Mahoe, all beautiful in their way, as certainly all are useful Mr. Ross, of Ruimveld, deserves the highest praise for the minute attention he has bestowed here; no one has done so much to bring out the capabilities of our fibres, and he has succeeded admirably. The prize awarded him is the least distinction he has earned by his zeal and care. He has tried the various processes, and exhibited the results, showing that carding with steel 011 wood is the best method for ensuring a tine long libre, and a showy colour. Iron on iron discolours the fibre, although it does not in any other way affect the value of the material. The silk grass libre is astonishingly fine, and its colour perfect. The rope made from it surpasses the Manilla in appearance þÿ and in durability, we be-

lieve it will be found to equal any other. The hammocks made by the Indians are of superior finish, and their lasting qualities are well known. The defect of the plantain fibre is that being a sharp instead of a round one, it cuts in knotting, but Ibis is readily overcome in the process of rope making, or weaving, which twists the fibre and so deprives it of its edge. Specimens of paper and of cloth from the plantain were also exhibited, showing its adaptability to an endless variety of purposes while Mr. Ross, with the same prescient view to the real aim of the exhibition, sent the long strips of the plantain stem, or flag, so highly prized by coopers for filling up the interstices of their work. We confess that these things struck us far more than the beautiful tables and articles of furniture exhibited, which being a limited selection of the best woods, showed nothing that was not previously known, and will naturally fail in Europe to excite attention, from this very circumstance. Had Sir. Delph taken the commonest woods, as well as the most perfect, and shown their capability of taking polish, and their usefulness generally and inlaid them in a different pattern, he would have succeeded far better. The effort is assuredly a most creditable one, and we are far from wishing to discourage him, but we wish to point out what will be to his advantage hereafter, as in another year he will have the opportunitv ofdisplaying his abilities again, the intention being to renew our exhibition

annually. The beautiful specimens of woods enlisted the attention of everyone, and we have the pleasure of record, ing the astonishment of a scientific observer, recently from Europe, who would scarce I v credit the evidence of his own senses at the profuse liberal ity with which nature has lavished her treasures upon this favored soil. The common Suradat i, which is perhaps the most ordinary wand we possess, used for planking stcliings, or the colonial craft, shows a polish like the face ot a mirror, and a grain closer than oak, while no insect will Ijve neurit from the bitter quality of the wood. Now, beyond the obvious use of these timbers, for ship

«jn « J sn 4 t n building and rough house work and furniture, would it not strike a European, that for public buildings, or large private houses, w here it was an object to make a great display, they would be eagerly sought for the stair cases, the doors, and the ornamental work every where, especially as they could be procured at a far cheaper rate than the costly woods, and might, if labor were abundant, be as cheap as deal. \\ e particularly desire to call attention to the fact, that the laboring class lias evinced a laudable anxiety to come forward and compete for prizes, and those who knew how proverbially slow the class is in every country in appreciating such a movement, will rejoice in the signs of awakening enterprise thus presented. We hope it will be sed dously inculcated on them that these exhibitions will be henceforth annual, and that no country in the West Indies can compete with this, if they be but faithful to as and to their own best interests. We trust, too, to see the Portuguese and the Immigrants generally, coming into the field next time, and showing how industry and ingenuity can turn anything to account. Above all things, we hope and trust that the colony will be fairly represented in the ensuing Paris Exhibition, for be sure it will lead to great results. Prance will, undoubtedly, turn her attention to Cayenne, and see that her own colonies are not behind hand in emulation, and unless England is willing to be outstripped in her productions, or to depend for her raw materials on

her enemies, she will not neglect us longer. England owes it to herself no less than to us to try to make our fibres available as a substitute for the hemp of Russia ; and as paper material is wanting, and the planting fibre produces several qualities of paper as well as cloth, why should it not be tried extensively. Instead of enriching an enemy, let England strive to bring on her own, and so ensure a return for herself. The chemical products were by no means adequately represented, being restricted to the Laurel Oil, the Rebenne, Citric Acid, by our friend Mr. Nicholl, a red vegetable ink, and a few other articles. The barks, too, were rather scantily shown, and one felt the want of persons who, like Mrs. Dennis, would lay themselves out to render their table doubly interesting by the kindness with which they explain every thing. It is no idle compliment to say that of a lady that she lias laid the community under an obligation by her courteous attention on the first days of the exhibition. Mrs. Wodehousc's valuable contributions from Central America and Ceylon, as Mr. Dennis' antiquities from the sepulchres of Elmsea, were much and deservedly admired; and although they might have been considered out of place in a merely colonial exhibition, we cannot but acknowledge the zeal and earnestness of the Commissioners, who have certainly laboured energetically and perseveringly to carry out their noble object becomingly. The eminent success oi the exhibition is their

best reward, and we right willingly pay them our tribute of gratitude and honor. Mr. Luckie displayed his rice in abundance, and we trust it will not fail to turn attention more decidly to this cultivation. The sugars, also, and the starch were magnificent specimens, both from their excellence and variety. The mango starch is a novelty, and another proof of the all but boundless wealth of the colony in its native produce. The crowds that thronged the rooms during the whole time behaved in the most orderly and decorous manner, and we feel assured that many, especially the young, will feel a new interest awakened in their hearts for the place of their birth, or of

their adoption. The live stock and vegetables and fruits were but by we no trust worthy of the occasion, menus tile failure of this first opening will be only a stimulus to a greater exertion hereafter. Next year should show a perfect Menagerie of the Colony's animals, birds, penance in reptiles, <fcc. his The solitary cage for his manifold ini- tiger doing quities, especially for his late unjustifiable eqnicide, is a fine specimen, but lie would have derived more interest trom being one of a series. (BY ELECTRIC TELEGRAPH ) THE CRIMEA, Jan. 14. The Turkish cavalry, now here, are to he sent to Eupatoria, and their embarkation lias begun. Considerable reinforcements have arrived at Balaklava, so that two new camps have been formed, which are being fortified. Gen. Liprandi has again pushed forward his outposts to the Tchernaya.

VIENNA. FRIDAY, Jan. 26. Intelligence fioin Constantinople up to the 18th January has been received. A contemplated insurrection of Softas has been discovered. An English transport, the Eveline, has been wrecked. The last dates from the Crimea are of Jan. 16. Nothing of importance had occurred.

BUCHAREST, Jan. 20. The Turks have established a recruiting bureau in Wallachia, in order to raise a Wallachian legion for the services of the Sultan. Prince Stirbey is preparing to go to Constantinople. A part of the Turkish force at Rem was sent to Kilia on the 16th inst.

ODESSA, Jan. 18. Prince Menschikoff, having received considerable reinforcements, estimated at 25,000 men, including the 8th division, 3d corps, lias determined to resume the offensive, and make another general attack on the Anglo-French lines, immediately after the return of the two Grand Dukes, for whose special edification this spectacle is reserved.

PARIS, Jan. 27. A FRENCH ARMY FOR AUSTRIA. It is freely stated in Paris that an ex- French army will forthwith proceed to the succour of Austria against the Russians. Some fix the amount at 100,000, some at 160,000, and the Imperial Guard, with the exception of one regiment. It is also confidently affirmed that this force would pass through Switzerland. The 5th of February is the date fixed for the commencement of its march.
FRANKFORT, Friday. The Committees of the German Diet met yesterday. Au-stria proposed the

mobilisation of the forces of the Federal States. Prussia opposed the entertaining of the question; other Federates required time to consult with their courts on various points. Hanover declared herself ready immediately to comply with the requisition of Austria. The Diet has, as yet, come to no decision.

THE EXTRAORDINARY GAZETTE OF YESTERDAY. The latest authentic accounts come down to the 13th of January, at which date a despatch lias just been received from Lord Raglan, announcing the continuance of the same cold and snowy weather. On the previous night, the 12th, the Russians made a sortie on the right and left attack of the British, under the protection of a heavy cannonade, along the \\ oronzow road and the ravine on the extreme left. The troops were driven in from the advanced trench, and a sergeant and 13 soldiers made prisoners, while an officer and 36 men were wounded. The disembarking and distribution of warm clothing continued, and Lord Raglan says, þÿ believe I I may assert that every man in this army has received a second blanket, a jersey frock, flannel drawers, and socks, and some kind of winter coat, in addition to the ordinary great þÿcoat. The providing of fuel was still a great difficulty, and the huts were being landed and put up, hut as they weighed each .two ions and a half, there was great difficulty, with their limited means, in getting them up to the camp. Much sickness still prevailed in the army. »» « «-« LATEST INTELLIGENCE FROM THE CRIMEA. Observer Office, Saturday, 3 þÿo clock.

The news from the Crimea comes down to the 10th. At that date nothing of importance had taken place before Sebastopol. On the 5th of January Omar Pasha was at the camp of the allies He concerted measures with the English and French commanders on the movements of the armies. On the 6th lie returned to Varna. He will immediately assume the direction of the operations intrusted to him. A despatch from Admiral Brunt, dated January 5, announces that the snow had fallen heavily, hut the sun shone again brightly. The thermometer was at 2 degrees below zero. North-easterly winds prevailed. On the 8th the Russians attempted a sally from Sebastopol, hut were driven hack with loss. The Ottoman army in the Crimea will he increased in the course of January to 60, 0U0 men. The completion of the last parallel of the English had been retarded t.y the snow. On the 25th of December Prince Menschikotr issued a general order, which has been also published at Simphcropol and Baktehi-serai It concludes with these words: þÿ þÿ By the help of God and our indomitable force we shall vanquish and annihilate our þÿenemies. 'I'll e loss of the Russians at Sebastopol and the neighbourhood during the last days of December is estimated at more than 6,000 men. þÿ Ibid Jan. 21.

ADHERENCE OF THE KING OF SARDINIA TO THE ALLIES. The assent of the King of Sardinia to the policy of the Western Powers in the present war is not confined to the mere adoption by the Court of Turin of the protocols and treaties which have been left open by the high contracting parties for the acceptance of the other States of Europe. The Sardinian Government

have resolved, with an energy which does them honour, and may well he contrasted with the irresolute policy of the Northern States of the continent, to take rio half-measures in this quarrel. They were no douht enabled, by their geographical position, to stand aloof altogether; but Count Cavour and his colleagues have thought that it was more conducive to the national interests of the monarchy to take an active and prominent part in this war. The result is, that Sardinia has not only acceded to the Treaty of the 2nd of December with Austria, England, ami France, hut lias also concluded a direct treaty of offensive and defensive alliance with the Western Powers, by virtue of which a corps of 15,000 Piedmontese troops will join the allies forces in the E ist. These troops are the descendants of the men who have for centuries upheld the military reputation of the house of Savoy, and who served with credit under Napoleon when their country was absorbed in the French empire. They are well known to be excellent soldiers, and they will, no doubt, prove a valuable addition to Lord þÿRaglan s army, to which this division will he more particularly attached. The Piedmontese Government will not receive any subsidy of war from this country, hut some assistance will lie given it in the negociation of a loan to meet the expenses of the expedition. Count Cavour has shown the extreme importance he attaches to the direction of the foreign relations of the Government at this crisis by taking tli :t branch

of t he administration into his own hands ; and it is already announced that communications of the highest importance will shortly he made to the Chambers now sitting at Turin. It is certainly a remarkable proof of the energy of the constitutional Government of Sardinia that, while it is engaged in a formidable struggle with the whole clerical and absolutist party for the secularization of the monasteries, it should take an ac live part in the general affairs of Europe, and commence its pre parations as a belligerent Power. þÿ Ibid.

Letters from Hamburg of the 16th instant state that, in consequence of the sudden setting in ot the frost with great rigour (the thermometer in the previous night having been down to 10 degrees Reaumur below zero), the river Elbe was tilling fast with floating ice, and the greatest bustle and activity were everywhere perceptible in the harbour to finish the loading of the outward bound ships and get them off before they were prevented by the ice. All the steamers for the different English and Scotch ports, whether loaded or not, would start the same evening. þÿ Ibid.

The hurricane which caused such havoc amongst life and property in the north of Germany on New þÿYear s Day appears to have had a diameter of about 600 miles. It took its rise in the Polar Seas, swept over the Orkneys and Shetland Islands, covered the whole of the North Sea, caused immense damage in Holland, Hanover, and Denmark, and went down to Prussia and Austria, where its fury broke. We understand that, on the evening of the 23rd instant, Lord John Russell wrote to the Earl of Aberdeen, intimating that Mr. Roebuck had given notice of a motion for the appointment of a committee to inquire into the conduct of the war. Lord John Russell stated that lie did not see how the motion could be resisted. And he added, that as it involved a censure upon the War Department, with which his colleagues were connected, he thought his only course was to tender his resignation. This resignation was carried to Windsor by Lord Aberdeen, on Wednesday, and has been accepted by her Majesty. We were right, therefore, when we yesterday predicted that Mr. þÿRoebuck motion s would lead to a Ministerial crisis. But the progress of events has been even more rapid than we expected. The break up of the Ministry has preceded, not followed, t he debate on Mr. R þÿoehuck mo- s tion. We say the breakup of the Ministry þÿ for the resignation of Lord John Russell is the drawing of the linch-pin out of the coalition coach ; it is impossible that the crazy vehicle can continue to 1 ru mi I e on. Lord John Russell having tendered his resignation, on the express ground that lie thought the national demand for inquiry into the conduct of the war ought to he complied with, Lord Aberdeen, by advising his Sovereign to accept the resignation, has declared his resolution to resist all inquiry. It is impossible with so many gross instances of mismanagement staring the public in
the face, and with such manifest impatience on the part of the nation to know the whole truth, as a preliminary to improved management, that any Ministry can make a stand on such untenable

ground. The truth is, that secresy and concealment can only tend to a perpetuation of imbecile formalism in the conduct of the war. They can only screen that cowardice which has occasioned all the delay and confusion mulct which the army in the Crimea is suffering ; cowardice, not of our armaments in the livid, lint of people at home, who have never dared to make one appointment for merit alone, nor to recall the itidiv idual tor incapacity or neglect. Under a system of secresy tio encouragement is held out to an English Ministry to make good appointments ; on the contrary, it ensures immunity from punishment, by making j had appointments; and is nothing short ofa national misfortune. It encourages a Minister to make bad appointments, inasmuch ns it enables him to make a show ot' vindicating himself by at any time throwing the blame upon some subj ordinate, and sacrificing the unfortunate to appease public indignation. This wretched system, we have good reason to believe, has been systematically acted upon by some of the Ministers, who have given countenance to the attacks upon Lord Raglan, from the ignoble motive of averting such attacks from themselves. Against this dastardly policy þÿ against the system of mystification and concealment which lias rendered its practice possible.

PAY YOUR DEBTS. Were I entrusted with authority to issue a mandate, in my judgment the best calculated for promoting the prosperity of the commercial interests of this country, it should he comprised in these few words, þÿ PAY As the commencement oftheyearis the usual time when tradesmen send in their hills, could an order to this effect be enforced, it would he found extremely beneficial. There is so much disappointment, and so many severe remarks cast upon each other by persons in trade, on account of the non-payment of accounts, that I think we should try, if possible, to effect a reform. Instead of gatory, because we have facilities for allowing your bills to remain unnoticed, and protracting the payments to the latest possible period, let me entreat you to examine them immediately, and at the foot of those which you find correct, make a remark to this effect, þÿ Ex þÿ to be paid.' þÿ Those which are not so, get adjusted as soon as possible. Then proceed forthwith according to your means, to the payment. Here 1 am aware in numerous instances, a difficulty will present itself I need not say that þÿ that this isþÿ the want of money. This arises in many cases wot from real poverty, or from a sufficient amount not being due, lint from the dishonesty or carelessness of numerous customers. A commercial community s l>ke a machine, an integral part of which cannot he tiiovei without the corresponding motion of other parts. It is of no use pumping when t here is no water in the well. There is a stream running in the

East of Lancashire, which propels the machinery of numerous establishments, situated on its banks at the distance of perhaps every half mile. Each establishment, to the distance of many miles, depends upon the same current. If any of those towards the rise of the rivulet, either through carelessness or self-interest were to detain the water, all helow would feel the inconvenience and he at a dead stand for want of power. But to use it in due course, allowing the same to flow as rapidly as the channel will permit, is paying a due regard to the interests of all, and is nothing less than what all the proprietors of the dependent establishments have a right to expect. Let men of capital apply this to themselves. Though there are many tradesmen who have no independent means, and whose payments depend simply upon the honesiv and promptitude of others, yet in þÿthis country we have a great number of real capitalists ; and it is from their cotfrs that the pleasant and gratifying impulse necessary for reciprocally settling accounts must proceed. þÿ Money, like þÿmanure, it has been said, þÿ does no good till it is þÿdistributed; and while thousands just now are in a state of suspense, scarcely knowing what course to pursue, it would be an act of generosity þÿ not to say justice þÿ for those who have money, instantly to settle to the utmost of their power, all outstanding accounts. The harmonious working of the commercial system depends wholly upon two particulars þÿ honesty and judicious i

arrangement. The former will teach a man that wilfully to withhold the payment of an account which is equitably due, is decidedly an act of injustice. Doubtless, the law may make a difference betwixt such an act and the possessing ourselves by force or stratagem of the property of another, but it is difficult to perceive a difference in the eye of strict justice. It is not doing as we would others should do to us. Again, a man may be honest in his intentions, and yet, careless and indiscreet. þÿ He may put others to great inconvenience, who, through fear of losing a connexion, dare

3 þÿ o i e> j :£ at j not utter a word of complaint. Most of the Christmas bills might as easily lapaid this present month as permitted to run, according to a bad custom, into another half year. Every conscientious person feels the happiest when he is out of debt ; having paid every man his own; YOUR þÿDEBTS. I and he who is regardless of this, is not merely doing an injury to the individuals whose hills are in his hands, but like the man who assists to poison the water at the fountain, is diffusing a sickly infection into the commercial body, which may help to produce in its distant results a national paroxysm called þÿ a þÿpanic. þÿ Owe no man any þÿthug is a Divine command ; and is not less obli-
breaking it without incurring that public odium which attaches to many other acts perhaps not more sinful in the sight of þÿGod. San Fernando Gazette.

What arc liixurics Tor a Wife. A novel case has just been decided in New York, which involves a curiosity in medico-juris-prudence. A mesmeric physician sued a husband for services rendered the wife in his absence. Toe Supreme Court say that the law does not recognise the dreams, visions, or revelations of a woman in a mesmeric sleep as necessaries for a wife, for which the husband, without his consent, can he made to pay. These are fancy articles which those who have money of their own to disposeofmaypurchase, if they think proper: hut they are not necessaries, known to the law, for which the wife can pled ire the credit of her absent husband. The law does not seem to have much respect for Mesmerism and Spiritrapping as sciences.

Communication. Mr. Printer! In your last number of the Avis you commented on the impropriety of permitting fishermen to torch on the reef I during the night. I believe you are mistaken if under ! the impression that this is done at late hours þÿ I believe never after 10 þÿo clock p. m., by which time trading vessels making for this port, will have had sufficient landmarks to go by. Hut what is most desirable, and would avert the danger of false lights, would be to have a proper light at the Newfort, which now twinkles for a time during the night and is only seen at some distance from the land, but miserable in hazy or squally weather. Prom among many amusing stories of his tact and dexterity, we select the following from the Pennsylvania Courier : þÿ Professor Anderson was playing in the Holyday-street theatre, Baltimore, to crowded houses every evening. On the last night of his appearance in the city, the hall was numerously thronged, and the Professor took occasion to introduce some new feats of more astonishing character than lie had previously shown. Among the audience, and occupying a prominent position in the middle of the hall, sat a sallow-complcxioned, hatchetface þÿ South þÿCarolinian, who regarded the performance very intently, but never joined in the applause awarded to the Wizard by the rest of the company. He. saw the Professor take a large trunk, two or three geese, and a live boy out of a portfolio about two inches thick, and he nodded as much as to say þÿ þÿ þÿThat s not quite so þÿbad. LORD CLARENDON rose and said, that he thought it bis duty to inform the house that he had received, about halt an hour ago, a telegraphic despatch from Her þÿMajesty Minister s at the Hague, announcing the death of the Emperor of Russia between 12 and I þÿo clock this morning. Emperor Nicholas had died of apoplexy, after a previous attack ot influenza. Though the event had occurred there could he no doubt of its truth. so short Considering, a time ago, therefore, lie apprehended that the influence this event might have on the negotiations now pending for the attainment of pence, lie hoped the noble Lord (Lord Lyndliurst) would not press bis motion for ibis evening. Lord LYNDHURST said that after the statement made by the noble earl, be could not refuse to withdraw bis motion. TO THE EDITOR OF THE TIMES. Total 17,404 One would have thought that Captain Chappell ought to have known what ships were so engaged. But as Captain Chappell has rushed into print to defend the monopoly he represents, I wish he had told the public what sum the Government had mulct from their 240,000/. per annum, which they still receive under their head of postal services, for þÿ the trifling amount of mileage which has been left unperþÿformed by them; and, further, why the company had no mails between this country and the Brazils during the month of December, which they were bound by their contract to have? During the whole of this dreary winter the works of the siege have been slowly but steadily advancing. After the wretched means of conveyance over impassa! le roads, which were insufficient to convey the daily rations of food to the front, were nevertheless appropriated to the transport of ammunition ; and all the strength of the army which has not been expended in its mortal struggle with the inclemency of the season and the ravages of disease has been applied to the works from which the fire of the besiegers was at last to re-open on the enemy. There is no doubt that the few fine days which have intervened since the disappearance of the heavy snow have allowed this labour to be carried on with increased effect, and we may now anticipate with some degree of confidence the recommencement of more active operations. It is obviously impossible that the allied armies can indefinitely retain their present positions; they cannot wait until the fine season enables the Russian army to move in large masses upon the Crimea, and the heats of summer breed a still more fatal pestilence than that which has hitherto devastated their camps. We infer, therefore, that the first measure of the Generals, to be taken at the earliest practicable moment, will he a combined bombardment of Sebastopol by laud and sea, to be followed, if possible, by an assault ; and, if this last attempt upon the place is foiled by the strength of the Russian defences, the only means of making good their posi-
tion in the Crimea will be to take the field þÿ in other words to raise the siege, and transfer the scene of war elsewhere.

From Me Observer, February 25, 1855. IIOUSE-FLESH AS FOOD. M. Geoft'roy Saint-llilaire, professor at the Museum of Natural History, has just delivered two lectures on the advantages of bringing horse-flesh into use for food. There is no reason, he declares, why horse-flesh should not he eaten like the ox and the sheep; the horse is herbivorous, and no deleterious element enters into its food or structure. Its flesh, besides, is full of azote. The ancient Germans and Scandinavians had a marked liking for horse-flesh. They preserved a certain race of white horses to be sacrificed to Odin, and after the sacrifice they boiled the flesh and feasted on it. The introduction of Christianity put an end to this custom, and probably led to the aversion to horse-flesh, which is now generally manifested in Europe. The nomade tribes of Northern Asia make horse-flesh their favourite food, though they have numerous flocks of oxen and sheep. In spite of the dislike of horse-flesh in modern Europe, the Danes have recommenced the use of it. During the siege of Copenhagen in 1807, the Government formally authorised the sale of it in butchers' shops, and since then it has been constantly sold ; there is, even in that city, a privileged slaughter-house for horses placed under the surveillance of the Veterinary þÿSchool and horse flesh is sold n it at the average price of 12c. per lb. Parent Duchatel, an esteemed writer, asserts that large quantities of horse-flesh were formerly introduced into Paris on different pretexts, lluzard, an eminent veterinary surgeon,

states that in the scarcity which followed the Revolution of 1789, the greater part of the meat consumed at Paris for six months was horse-flesh, and that it caused no ill-effect on the public health. The distinguished army surgeon, liaron Larrey, made his wounded patients eat horse-flesh in the campaigns of the Rhine, of Catalonia, and of the Maritime Alps, and he ascribes to it the cure of a great number of his sick in Egypt. From all these facts, and numerous others, M.Geoffroy Saint-Hilairc insisted that the horse, in addition to the services which it already renders to man, can be made to supply cheap and nutritious food

As closely cropped hair is a punishment for immoral conduct, and exposes a girl to the jeers and reproaches of her compapanions, it may be imagined what a bitter mortification this is. I must, however, in justice, say that the lady was a Pole. I was once going to the Opera, and the lady of the house begged me to wait a few minutes, as she was not quite ready. She went into her cabinet de toilette, and suddenly 1 heard a tremendous noise, and the lady and her maid endeavouring to out-scold each other. j employes Presently there was a loud crash, and a fall of something heavy on the floor; and the lady soon after rejoined me smiling, and apologising for keeping me waiting. I subsequently learned that the maid had not pleased in her coiffure ; the lady scolded, and the maid answered impertinently, and her amiable mistress was so enraged that she took the chair on which she was sitting and knocked her down with great violence, breaking two of her front teeth. Centuries of warfare and mutual cruelties have caused these two groat divisions of the same race to hate each other with the greatest intensity. And yet every Polish gentleman is forced to take an oath, in which he calls on Heaven to witness that

he will shed the last drop of his blood for the Emperor's sake. It must be galling to have to pronounce these words with the recollections of the wrongs of his country, and the remembrance of an outraged mother or sister, publicly flogged for instilling sentiments of patriotism into his soul. Let it not be thought that these are merely words. Many a time I have been told of Polish ladies who have been sufferers from the executioner's lash not many years ago in the capital. Hundreds of instances of the kind have been told to me. 1 asked a noble Pole one day how he could take such an oath; and his answer was, that they made a reservation of their allegiance to themselves-that they believed in Poland's resurrection, and could do present. In every part of Russia numbers of Poles arc found who have been banished their country for some political offence, although they never had been confronted with their accusers, never been accused, and had ofcourse no means of proving their innocence. In Warsaw the people are all under the despotic rule of the Russian employes and spies, who treat them with the greatest cruelty.

In giving publicity to the above, which is taken from the lists niatle out bv the respective Burgher Councils in St. Croix, St. Thomas and St. Johns, we begin Call attention to the 13th $ of the Colonial Law, which points out the means for the rectification of any faults or omissions in the lists. The paragraph runs thus: "should the name of any person, who does not possess the qualifications, which entitle to vote, be found on the list, or any person wrongly be omitted in the same, any one may give notice in writing thereof to the superintendent of the poll (the judge in the elective district) and produce the necessary evidence at least 3 days previous to the election, and the superintendent shall summon not only the person, to whom the notice refers and to whom he shall hand a copy of the same, hut also the person by whom the objection has been made." The lists contain the electors
they represent, and therefore n person named in any of the lists, is eligible in all the districts.
